body.translated_text: <s>Siddhārthacaritra Kāvya</s> (The Poem of the Life of <s>Siddhārtha</s>), composed by Ācārya <s>Buddhaghoṣa</s>, the <s>Padyacūḍāmaṇi Mahākāvya</s> (Great Poem, Crest-Jewel of Verse).
First Canto: <s>Maṅgala</s> (Auspicious Beginning)

children.translated_text: Whose compassionate glance overflows with waves [of mercy], who is a dark cloud [that extinguishes] the fire of <s>Kandarpa</s>'s (Love's) pride,
Who is the root-bulb of the wish-fulfilling tree of liberation — I salute that great <s>Kandala</s> (bulb), kinsman of the sun.
Even sages such as the lotus-seated one (<s>Brahmā</s>) were not able to tell even a fraction [of his deeds];
That I presume to tell the life-story of the Teacher — this is merely my folly.
Yet, with the power of devotion placed in him, I am skilled enough to narrate this;

children.text: tathāhi tatpādasamāśrayeṇa rajo 'pi lakṣmīṃ kurute hi puṃsām // 1.3 //
children.translated_text: For by taking refuge at his feet, even dust brings prosperity to men.

children.text: asti praśastā kapileti nāmnā kācit purī kāmadughā prajānām /
children.translated_text: There is a renowned city called <s>Kapilā</s> (Kapilavastu), a wish-fulfilling [cow] for its people,

children.text: yāṃ vīkṣya śakro nijarājadhānyāḥ ślāghābhisandhiṃ śithilīkaroti // 1.4 //
children.translated_text: Seeing which, <s>Śakra</s> (<s>Indra</s>) loosens his pride in his own royal capital.
Where the moon is honored — its orb clinging to the flagstaffs of the mansions ���
As if impaled on a trident by the women, in anger at [the moon] robbing the radiance of their lotus-faces.

children.text: vīthīṣu māṇikyamayīṣu yasyāṃ jyotīṃṣi bhānti pratibimbitāni /
children.translated_text: In whose streets paved with gems, the reflected lights shine
As if they were pearls fallen from the bow of <s>Anaṅga</s> (the bodiless god of love), plucked [from the bowstring].
Where the lofty houses of the wealthy, bearing the staffs of upraised victory banners,
Constantly invite [visitors] to receive [gifts], as it were, with the tinkling of their swinging bells.

children.text: rathyāsu ratnopahitāsu yasyāṃ bimbapraviṣṭāḥ kariṇo vibhānti /
children.translated_text: Where on the jewel-inlaid streets, elephants reflected [in the surface] appear
Like mountain peaks of the shore-mountains descending to assist the lord of serpents (<s>Kuṇ���alīndra</s>).
Where the dolls in the latticed windows of the houses, wrought with heaps of gold,
Enhance the splendor of city-guardian deities brought from conquered enemy cities.
Where separated women, ascending the mansions that surpass the paths of clouds,

children.text: kathānabhijñā dhanagarjitānāṃ vasanti yasyāṃ vanitā viyuktāḥ // 1.10 //
children.translated_text: Dwell even on dark rainy days, unknowing of the tales of [mere] thunder of wealth.
Where the dwellings, with their upraised golden banner-staffs like exceedingly long arms,
Seem to snatch away, as if jealous, the splendor of the mansions of <s>Śunāsīra</s>'s (<s>Indra</s>'s) city.
Where the women, taking hold of the crescent moon near the rooftops [i.e., reflected in them],
And placing it in their tresses, rival the beauty of <s>Ambikā</s> (<s>Pārvatī</s>).
Where the pavilions, heated by the intense summer, with their waving banner-edges,
Seem to savor the cool-rayed moon with the nectar of their whitewashed surfaces, relishing its orb.

children.text: vilokya caityadhvajasiṃhamudrāṃ bhayākule kvāpi gati kuraṅge /
children.translated_text: Where, upon seeing the lion-seal on the <s>caitya</s> (shrine) banner, a deer somewhere in panicked flight —
The moon attains resemblance to the faces of the beauties, [both being] lotus-like.
Where in the moonlit galleries, as the women's attendants perform the play of adornment,
The full moon's orb approaching [the mirror] assumes the role of a mirror in the nights.
Where the expanding rays streaming from the sapphire-stone gateways
Create, for a moment, the suspicion of a dark spot even on the sheltering sun's orb.
Where the rivers, with pleasure-hills on their banks reflected in their clear waters,
Assume the beauty of the celestial <s>Mandākinī</s> (Ganges) with divine elephants submerged in the heat of rut.
Where the rays, high and low, rising from the jewel-built houses,
Make the sky appear armed with celestial bows even after the rainy season has ended.
The women of that [city], who have begun their play on the golden palace terraces,
Eclipse the radiance of the celestial nymphs sporting on the peaks of <s>Meru</s>.
Where the spreading lustre-vines of the crystal-studded mansions
Seem to become momentary fly-whisks for the ears of the green horses [of the sun] nearby.
Where, with the far-flung rays of the jeweled arches pouring forth streams of light,
The heavenly <s>Gaṅgā</s> seems to shine through the sky, its interior mottled by the daughter of <s>Kalinda</s> (<s>Yamunā</s>).
Where on the rooftops of the mansions, the lofty fish-banners trembling in the wind
Struggle angrily against the <s>makaras</s> (crocodiles) of the aerial <s>Gaṅgā</s>, mistaking them for rivals.
Where the fatigue of lovemaking of the beauties who have ascended cloud-touching palaces
Is gently removed by the breeze that sports among the waves of the <s>Mandākinī</s>.
Where the full moon, with its cluster of digits complete, ruler of the nectar-ray,
Seems to anoint with its ray-like sprouts the upper terraces of the pleasure-houses in the nights.
Where swans, seeing the first crescent moon reflected in the sapphire-paved [floors],
Strain with their bills to nibble it, craving [what looks like] a piece of lotus stalk.
Where, seeing the mass of incense-smoke rising from the houses — which, thick and sudden, looks like <s>Rāhu</s> —
The lord of days (the sun), out of fear, hides himself among the cloud-forests.
Where the curved beauties of the lovely women, reflected in the crystal floors,
Create the illusion of lotuses blooming in the waters of the sky-river.
Where even the lord of lights (the sun), unable to pass beyond its rampart — which puts the <s>Cakravāla</s> (world-mountain range) to shame —
Travels by the pretext of the northern and southern halves [of the sky] alongside its walls.
Where the moat, with waves swelling from the agitation of the wind, overrunning the banks,
Seems to make an effort to conquer the <s>Kalaśa</s> (pot-like) ocean [i.e., the cosmic ocean].
Where the silk victory-banners of the mansions, mingled with dark <s>agaru</s> (aloe) incense, sing —
Like garlands of waves of the heavenly <s>Gaṅgā</s>, daughter of the sun, their crests broken by billows.
In that [city] there was a venerable king, of the <s>Śākya</s> lineage, possessing eternal royal splendor,
Whose livelihood was pure through earning in accordance with <s>dharma</s> — named <s>Śuddhodana</s>, a name true to its meaning.

children.text: vibhuḥ pratāpānalameva vīdhraṃ vivāhasākṣye viracayya vīraḥ /
children.translated_text: The mighty hero, having made the fire of his prowess itself the witness to his marriage,
Married the royal splendor of his enemies, preceded by a libation of sword-edge water [i.e., blood].
He who, having first performed the great consecration with elephant-pots dripping with blood,
Then nourished the worship of the war-goddess with the heart-lotuses of his enemies.

children.text: pāṇau kṛpāṇī virarāja yasya vibhūṣitāṅgī pulakākṣareṇa /
children.translated_text: In whose hand the sword shone, her body adorned with letters of gooseflesh,
Like a decree sent by <s>Yama</s> to summon his enemies.
Whose moonlike smile, having suppressed the excess of glory of [rival] kings, having drunk up the armies of his foes entirely,
Gave rise to the pacification of the world, like <s>Agastya</s> by his rising [who swallowed the ocean and pacified the demons].
Who, like a cloud that has grasped its bow [the rainbow], raining upon the enemy king's mountain-army,
Made [their army], with its royal swans [i.e., elephants] bewildered, perform the dance of headless trunks [i.e., slaughter].
Where ghouls, adorning themselves with garlands of warriors' entrails, taking the trunks [of elephants] like horns,
Performed the play of sprinkling in the rivers [of blood] reddened by his enemies' [blood].
For [receiving] the collyrium of the fame of his praiseworthy bride, that excellent [king] ��
The sky, dense and dark, appeared like a sapphire vessel set in place.
When the sky was filled to the brim with his fame that pervaded the world-egg's hollow,
There was, as it were, no room for the fame of other kings to spread.
If his fame, white as the cool-rayed moon, had not existed as a cooling remedy,
How could this world have endured the irresistible fire of his prowess?

children.text: bhujena bhogīndradhurandhareṇa yasmin dṛḍhaṃ bhūvalayaṃ dadhāne /
children.translated_text: When he held the earth's girdle firmly with his arm, which bore the burden like the great serpent-king,
From the creeper-arms of his adversaries' wives fell varied ornamental bangles.
Having taken refuge in that supremely generous one, suppliants sought no other;
Having reached the ocean, do the rivers desire any other lake!
On the terrace of his shoulders, where the garland is a canopy and the wine flows, making it thoroughly cool,
<s>Lakṣmī</s> (Fortune) played as if released from her veil, feverish from the heat of [his] valor outside.
At his consecration, by the waters brought from the holy <s>Gaṅgā</s> and other sacred places, released by his ministers,
The fever in people's hearts was quenched together with the fire-power of his enemies' valor.
Golden in form, served by good minds, lofty, the abode of excellent <s>dharma</s>, without a second —
The six treasures of virtues, having taken refuge in that king as if in <s>Meru</s>, shone brilliantly.
Though the ear was engaged elsewhere among the wise, it clung to hearing his deeds;

children.text: apāsya pīyūṣarasaṃ surāṇāṃ rasāntare kiṃ ramate rasajñā! // 1.46 //
children.translated_text: Having set aside the nectar-juice of the gods, does the connoisseur delight in any other flavor!
Though there were thousands of other kings, the earth was well-governed only through him;
The ocean, source of many gems, became known as 'Mine of Gems' only through the <s>Kaustubha</s>, did it not?
Since the nectar-eaters (gods) were constantly invited by that great soul's sacrifices,
The <s>Pārijāta</s> tree became merely an ornament of the lord of gods' capital.
His deeds, being sung by celestial women standing on the [mountain-]banks,
Even <s>Meru</s> seems to melt with joy, on the pretext of its flowing waters, to this day.
When that king showered the rain of gifts, not a single person remained with an unfulfilled desire;
When the great cloud rains with unbroken streams, is there a lake on earth that remains unfilled!

children.text: nadīva sindhornalinīva bhānoḥ kaleva cendoḥ kamaleva viṣṇoḥ /
children.translated_text: Like a river to the ocean, like a lotus to the sun, like a digit to the moon, like <s>Kamalā</s> (<s>Lakṣmī</s>) to <s>Viṣṇu</s>,

children.text: saudāminīvāmbudharasya tasya māyeti nāmnā mahiṣī babhūva // 1.51 //
children.translated_text: Like lightning to the cloud — his queen was [a woman] named <s>Māyā</s>.
Her pair of lotus-feet bore, with a radiance like the belly of a coral,
Full-moon toenails that made the creeper-tresses of vassal queens blossom [with desire to worship them].
The expanding jewel-radiance of the nails of her feet, [she being] one whose lord was her deity,
Created the suspicion that the moonlight, seeking refuge [there], feared [being swallowed by] <s>Svarbh��nu</s> (<s>Rāhu</s>).
Displaying a form of most wondrous composition and manifest delicacy,
Of those two shanks of hers, possessing such radiance — nothing was superior, nor even equal.

children.text: ye darśanīyā dviparājahastā ye cābhijātāḥ kadalīviśeṣāḥ /
children.translated_text: What are the beautiful hands of a young elephant, what are the excellent banana stems —
They are [mere] drops from the ocean of beauty that swells forth from the pair of her thighs.
The king's lawful wife, bearing the weight of her hips encircled by a ruby girdle,
[Was] like the earth, with its sandy shores embraced by the gem-womb ocean.
The navel-hollow of the slender-browed [queen] appeared with a beauty as charming as the whirlpool of the divine ocean,
As if it were a place made low by the cascades of the river of radiance flowing from her breast-mountains.
For the body-field of hers, rich with the crop of <s>Anaṅga</s> (Love), to be irrigated with the waters of beauty's flow,

children.text: āsūtritā yauvanahālikena trayīva kulyā trivalī cakāśe // 1.58 //
children.translated_text: The triple fold [of skin at the waist], like a threefold irrigation channel, fashioned by the farmer of Youth, shone forth.
Her [waist], clinging, with three folds attached, the birthplace of poverty [i.e., slender],
Appeared like the sky embraced by the braided streams of the celestial <s>Gaṅgā</s>.
The line of fine new body-hair, dark as a <s>tamāla</s> tree, of that lotus-eyed one,
Seemed like a rising column of portent-smoke, revealing the destruction of [her] childhood state.
As [Love] extended his archery lesson in the mind of the tender-limbed [queen],
The fine line of body-hair of the slender one appeared like a bowstring that had gone outside [the body] as a reflection.
With the swelling sphere of her breasts of that young woman, transgressing its bounds,
Having entirely occupied its own space, [the garment] remained clinging only in what was left.
The lotus-stalk of the playful pond, the lightning-creeper of the cloud-bank of youth,
the auspicious garland of <s>Makaradhvaja</s> (Kāmadeva, the god of love) — the arm of the doe-eyed one shone. // 1.63 //
Wearing a necklace of released pearls, beautiful to behold, her neck shone exceedingly,
like a wave of the ocean, brilliant with conch shells, adorned with heaps of spat-out pearls. // 1.64 //
Then, by <s>Pitāmaha</s> (Brahmā, the Grandfather), wishing to create a moon without rival on earth,
a lotus was surely made, its fragrance captured, and the orb of the moon [was left] with an inner stain. // 1.65 //
Tree-sprouts, due to their unsteady delicacy, and ocean-corals, due to their rigid hardness,
could not enter into a comparison with the <s>bimba</s>-fruit lips of that lotus-eyed one. // 1.66 //
The radiance of her <s>bimba</s>-fruit lower lip, scattered by her playful smile,
shone like the twilight, with the glow of <s>bandhuka</s> flowers, its arrangement tinged by moonbeams. // 1.67 //
The great channel of overflowing beauty from the crescent moon of her utterly lovely forehead,
the parting-line of her hair, the bridge between the rivers of her eyes — the nose of the youthful one shone. // 1.68 //
Her cheek, with leaf-designs traced in musk, possessing the beauty of the moon’s disc,
surpassed and displaced the beauty of a mirror whose surface was clouded by the winds of clouds. // 1.69 //

children.text: babhūva tasyā nayanotpalasya nīlotpalasyāpi mahān viśeṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: Between her eye-lotus and a blue lotus, there was a great distinction:

children.text: amoghamastraṃ kusumāyudhasya pūrvaṃ dvitīyaṃ tu tapaḥsu śīrṇam // 1.70 //
children.translated_text: the former was the unerring weapon of the flower-armed one (<s>Kāmadeva</s>), while the latter was shattered in [the flames of] austerity. // 1.70 //
Defeated by her wide, playfulness-laden glance,

children.text: adyāpi vāsaṃ vanakandareṣu hriyeva kurvanti kuraṅgaśāvāḥ // 1.71 //
children.translated_text: even now, young deer dwell in forest caves, as if out of shame. // 1.71 //
With the waves of the ocean of good fortune, the branches of the wish-fulfilling tree of youth —
her eyebrow-creepers made her face appear like a lotus [attended] by rows of bees. // 1.72 //
The forehead-line of the lotus-eyed one shone, ending in curled locks,
like a banner-strip of <s>Anaṅga</s>’s (Kāmadeva’s) victory, with a row of barely visible letters and dots. // 1.73 //
Her face, captivating with its pair of restless glances, achieved comparison
with a lotus in which a pair of fish swim about within, submerged. // 1.74 //
She shone, her complexion golden like <s>gorocanā</s> (yellow orpiment), her tresses dark like bees,
like an auspicious lamp of honorable rising, its upper portion greyed by the rising smoke. // 1.75 //

body.text: ardhāsikāṃ bharturananyalabhyāṃ bhadrāsane saiva paraṃ prapede //
body.translated_text: She alone attained the supreme half-seat of her lord, unobtainable by any other.
What other women deserve — setting aside <s>Lakṣmī</s> — the dwelling on the chest of <s>Madhusūdana</s> (Viṣṇu)? // 1.76 //

children.translated_text: The king, desiring a son from that queen who shone with praiseworthy virtues,
became devoted to the worship of the deities with lamps, incense, and other offerings. // 1.77 //

children.text: mamajja tīrtheṣu jajāpa mantraṃ tatāna dānāni tapaścakāra /
children.translated_text: He bathed in sacred waters, recited <s>mantras</s>, extended gifts, and performed austerities;

children.text: śuśrāva dharmaṃ sujanaṃ siṣeve sa putrahetoḥ saha dharmapatnyā // 1.78 //
children.translated_text: he listened to the <s>dharma</s> and served virtuous people, together with his queen, for the sake of a son. // 1.78 //

children.text: iti gatavati puṇyairdīrghadīrghe 'pi kāle, patiravanipatīnāṃ putraratnaṃ na bheje /
children.translated_text: Though a very long time passed with [the accumulation of] merit, the lord of kings did not obtain the jewel of a son;

children.text: tadapi ca vavṛdhe tatprārthanā tasya puṃsāṃ viramati na hi yatnaḥ kāryasiddheḥ purastāt // 1.79 //
children.translated_text: yet his longing for that only grew, for effort does not cease before the accomplishment of the goal. // 1.79 //

body.text: iti buddhaghoṣācāryaviracite padyacūḍāmaṇināmni mahākāvye siddhārthacarite prathamaḥ sargaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the first <s>sarga</s> (canto) of the <s>Siddhārthacarita</s>, the great poem named <s>Padyacūḍāmaṇi</s>, composed by <s>Ācārya Buddhaghoṣa</s>.

Second <s>sarga</s> (canto):
The gods’ journey to <s>Tuṣitapurī</s> (the city of Tuṣita heaven)

children.text: tatrāntare jagati pūrvanimittamāsīd dṛṣṭvā tadadbhutamamartyagaṇāḥ sametāḥ /
children.translated_text: Meanwhile, an omen appeared in the world; having seen that wonder, the hosts of immortals assembled;

children.text: sarvajñatāvasara eṣa taveti vaktuṃ jagmuḥ purīṃ suragurostuṣitāabhidhānam // 2.1 //
children.translated_text: saying ‘This is the occasion for your omniscience,’ they went to the city called <s>Tuṣitā</s>, [the abode] of the preceptor of the gods. // 2.1 //
[They went to that city] whose sky was made verdant by the spreading splendor of its lofty sapphire palaces,
whose environs had the moon as a companion, rising alongside the shifting glances of playful young deer. // 2.2 //
Whose palace turrets and balconies had sprouts of rays being playfully licked by the tongues of <s>cakora</s> birds,
and whose appearance was like a garland of salutations strung by the long rays of jeweled arches extending horizontally. // 2.3 //
Where the eyes of women travelers on the road were set in motion by the twanging sounds of the bowstring of the five-arrowed one (<s>Kāmadeva</s>) [suggested by tinkling ornaments],
and whose streets were muddied by the stream of rut-fluid flowing from the temples of pride-maddened elephants of the quarters. // 2.4 //
Where the lamp-rows were rekindled by the bodily radiance of lotus-eyed women [beautiful as] a thousand [flashes of] lightning,
and where the women of the directions seemed veiled by silk banners (<s>vaijayantī</s>) raised high atop the mansions. // 2.5 //
Where the groups of women bending to gather flowers made the pleasure-hills seem sculpted by the swell of their full breasts,
and where the waters of the ponds seemed redundant, augmented by the streams of nectar dripping from <s>mākanda</s> (mango) buds. // 2.6 //
Where the beauty of <s>Śatakratu</s>’s (Indra’s) rainbow was gathered by the radiance of fresh gems atop the canopy of the bower of love,
and where the mention of poverty was abolished by <s>mandāra</s>, <s>kalpa</s>, <s>haricandana</s>, <s>pārijāta</s>, and <s>santāna</s> [wish-fulfilling] trees. // 2.7 //

children.text: tatra sthitaṃ suragaṇā dadṛśastamenaṃ siṃhāsane vividharatnaśilānibaddhe /
children.translated_text: There, upon a throne fashioned of various precious stones, the hosts of gods beheld him,
resplendent in manifold mineral hues, like the lord of beasts upon a slope of <s>Meru</s>. // 2.8 //
With a venerable, auspicious white parasol stationed near the ruby-crested balcony,
he rivaled the beauty of the eastern mountain, where the full moon is visible beside its jewel-summit. // 2.9 //
With the expansive forehead like a slab of freshly-wrought gold, and with sacrificial fires spreading all around it,
he seemed to distribute the nectar of radiance to adorn the faces of [women] with eyes as wide as the directions. // 2.10 //
With side-glances long and ample, playing in the waters of the waves of boundless compassion,
he seemed to produce rows of pleasure-lotuses in the directions for the royal splendor of the lord of the immortals. // 2.11 //
With gentle, blissful smiles of surpassing serenity, spreading through the caverns and hollows of space,
he seemed to create an eternal moon-world to augment the ocean of his own fame. // 2.12 //
With the company of friends nearby, whose beauty of unfeigned devotion resembled his own reflection,
in conversation, he seemed to pour forth affection, visible from the coral-red radiance of his lower lip and the [affection] shining from within. // 2.13 //
With glances blurred by tears of joy, his cheek adorned with bristling <s>pulaka</s> (horripilation),
he was listening to his own noble deeds being sung before him by a troupe of performers. // 2.14 //
With streams of nectar spilling from ear-ornaments fashioned from the blossoms of <s>kalpa</s> trees [and] garlands offered [to him],
he seemed to perform the ceremony of heroic consecration for the noble valor of his two arms. // 2.15 //
With his pair of lofty arms [like] mountain-born [peaks] giving rise to the doubt of [whether they are] the sun of splendor and the moon of fame,
he adorned his charming cheeks with a pair of auspicious earrings fashioned of rose-colored and white opals. // 2.16 //
With a garland fashioned from buds of <s>mandāra</s> flowers, hanging from the middle of his honored arm,
he seemed to display the descent of the power of <s>Maitrī</s> (loving-kindness), like a stream of red [nectar] issuing from the channel of his throat. // 2.17 //
With arms from which arose sprays of rays from released jewel bracelets, delighting the mind with reddish hue,
he seemed to bear his two arms as branches with sprouts of the light of his own valor bursting forth and covering [all]. // 2.18 //
With limbs anointed abundantly with <s>haricandana</s> (yellow sandalwood) paste, and with <s>kuṅkuma</s> (saffron) leaf-designs within,
he seemed to display the condition of <s>Jīmūtavāhana</s>, whose body was torn by the beak of <s>Garuḍa</s>, the king of birds. // 2.19 //
With rays [like] staffs of light from the gems of various ornaments, spreading all around in the circles of the directions,
he seemed to practice the burden of displaying the <s>ṛddhi</s> (supernatural powers) that were signs of the glory of the station of <s>Bodhi</s> (Enlightenment) to come. // 2.20 //
With the radiance of his ornaments cascading from his lotus-feet downward, [like] the splendor of ruby and plantain-hue,
from that [point] onward, he seemed to practice the art of wearing the saffron robe, the mark of the sage-hood that was to come. // 2.21 //
With the beautiful chest-plate, [reflecting like] a jewel doll of a mansion’s balcony,
he assumed the appearance of the slayer of <s>Kaiṭabha</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>), in whose chest directly dwells the king of the ocean’s daughter (<s>Lakṣmī</s>). // 2.22 //
With a red lotus in hand, caressed by the waters of his palm, overflowing with unceasing nectar,
he was recognized as King <s>Śibi</s>, whose eye-lotus was reddened by blood flowing immediately upon being plucked out. // 2.23 //
The bees, greedy for the spreading fragrance of the sandalwood paste anointing [his body], crowding the dark [bee-] assembly all around,
he seemed to be dispersing with that very [fragrance] the darkness within, thick as the darkness of ignorance, in all directions. // 2.24 //
With streams of the nectar of beauty of wondrous form, praiseworthy and spreading toward the mouths of the directions,
he seemed to flood the world of the king of immortals, nearby and afflicted by the heat of the sun of his own majesty. // 2.25 //
With the clinking sounds of the bangles on his radiant arms making vocal all the circles of <s>Hari</s> (Viṣṇu)’s attendants on every side,
he was fanned by a circle of white <s>cāmaras</s> (fly-whisks) [wielded] by the courtesans of the celestial city from afar. // 2.26 //
With his chest, which bore a beautiful necklace with rows of stars as pendants, resembling the sky,
embraced by the waves of the celestial river, he seemed to illuminate the cliffs of the mountain of the immortals. // 2.27 //
With a wondrous footstool fashioned of unbroken <s>padmarāga</s> (ruby) [petals] in the shape of lotuses,
its radiance surpassing the humbled treasure-lord of lotuses, he touched [it] with his left foot. // 2.28 //
With rays of his rosy toes rising forth, rivaling the luster of the soles of his lotus-feet,
he seemed to shower the light of the early morning sun to awaken the lotus-faces of the worshiping gods. // 2.29 //
With a fresh web of rays from his toenails, fleshy as the digits of the moon,
his lotus-feet seemed like [those of] the lotus-naveled one (<s>Viṣṇu</s>), beautiful with streams of nectar flowing from the celestial river. // 2.30 //

children.text: saṃsāreghoraparitāpajuṣāṃ janānāṃ saṃrakṣaṇāya kimayaṃ samayo na veti /
children.translated_text: 'Is this the time or not for the protection of beings afflicted by the terrible anguish of <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclic existence)?' —
as if wishing to descend even for a moment, with an inquiry [reflected in] the surface like a jeweled floor. // 2.31 //
Having seen the teacher of the three worlds, the gods bowed with their heads low, like the <s>pārijāta</s> tree of <s>Tuṣita</s> heaven bent far down,
and the gods, surpassing the realm of speech, began to honor him with hymns of praise. // 2.32 //
O Lord of the gods! Favor us with your sidelong glances, which are great channels for the flood of compassion surging within [your] gaze upon the afflicted,
and which are [like] ear-ornaments bearing the seal of awakened lotuses. // 2.33 //
O you whose body is embraced by the swelling waves of the ocean of milk of beauty surging freely,
O crest-jewel of the deities of <s>Tuṣita</s> heaven! Homage to you, devoted to the vow of supreme compassion! // 2.34 //
To you who are fulfilled with the surpassing honor of the coronation-garland of <s>Prajñā</s> (Wisdom), the foremost queen,
to you who delight in the festive discourse of drinking the nectar of the story of the supreme <s>āśrama</s> (stage of life), O ocean of virtues, homage! // 2.35 //

To you whose [chest is] adorned with markings [like those] of crocodile-hued [patterns] of the sandalwood paste [representing] the burden of the breasts of <s>Maitrī</s> (Loving-Kindness), your consort,
to you whose caverns between the directions are set in waves by [your] splendor, O ground for the ripening of the fortune of the three worlds, homage! // 2.36 //
To you who are the ship of <s>dharma</s> upon the ocean of beings, blazing with the submarine-fire flames of <s>Māra</s>’s prowess,
to you whose edict is crowned by the guardians of the heavens, O you of directional majesty, O sole teacher of the world, homage! // 2.37 //
O you of vast gaze, held by the edges of the waves of the flood of irremediable compassion flowing forth,
O you whose mind’s activity is set in waves by the nectar of <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation), O god of gods, sole eye of the world, homage! // 2.38 //
O you whose unbounded torrents of streaming tears have quenched the fire in the bellies of starving <s>rākṣasas</s> (demons),
O holder of the thread of creation devoted to the play of <s>nirvāṇa</s> (liberation), delightful to the eyes! O king of the gods! Homage, homage to you! [2.39]
To him whose streams of fame, sung by the women of the <s>Gandharva</s> (celestial musician) king, have flooded all directions,
who is devoted to protecting the worthy, whose fortune is ever-increasing — O <s>Bhagavān</s> (Blessed One), obeisance to you! [2.40]
O you whose ever-flowing great generosity, blameless in its splendor, surpasses the divine wish-fulfilling tree and the wish-granting cow,
who is of pure intention, adorned with good conduct — homage to you, O bearer of the burden of the world of <s>Tuṣita</s> (the heaven of contentment)! [2.41]
To him whose face, lovely as the orb of the full moon's nectar-rays, has humbled the glory of the finest lotus,
who is of tranquil mind, who has crushed the arm-strength of the one whose banner bears the fish (<s>Kāma</s>, the god of desire) — homage to you, O honored lord of sages! [2.42]
Him whose arm-staff humbles the trunk of the resplendent great elephant in rut, adorning the vast quarters,
whose beautiful lotus-face blossoms with loveliness — we worship you alone, O bestower of boons, O king! [2.43]

children.text: vīra! tvameva vijitākhiladiṅmukhasya mīnadhvajasya vinipātavidhau vidagghaḥ /
children.translated_text: O hero! You alone are skilled in bringing about the downfall of the fish-bannered one (<s>Kāma</s>), who has conquered all directions.

children.text: siṃhād ṛte jagati kaḥ khalu dhīracetā dantāvalaṃ jayati jarjaritādrikūṭam // 2.44 //
children.translated_text: Who in this world besides a lion, firm of heart, can vanquish an elephant that has shattered mountain peaks? [2.44]
You alone are capable of removing all the torment of hatred from the world, O mass of merit for those who seek refuge!

children.text: dhārādharaṃ taralavidyutamantareṇa dāvānalaṃ śamayituṃ bhuviḥ kaḥ kṣameta! // 2.45 //
children.translated_text: Without a rain-cloud bearing flickering lightning, who on earth could extinguish a forest fire? [2.45]

children.text: mohāndhakāramuṣitāni jagattrayāṇi puṇyādhika! tvamasi bodhayituṃ pravīṇaḥ /
children.translated_text: O you of surpassing merit! You are skilled at awakening the three worlds, whose [vision] has been stolen by the darkness of delusion.

children.text: ko vā vikāsayitumarhati kokabandhuṃ bhānuṃ vinā śaradi paṅkajakānanāni // 2.46 //
children.translated_text: Who but the sun, friend of the day-lotus, is able to make the lotus-groves bloom in autumn? [2.46]
To dry up the flood of craving in people, O lord of the radiant ones, you alone are most capable.
Without the submarine fire at the end of the <s>kalpa</s> (cosmic age), who in the world could drink up the lord of waters (the ocean)? [2.47]

children.text: dhīra! tvameva jananāmbunidhestrilokīṃ pāraṃ paraṃ gamayituṃ paṭutāmupaiṣi /
children.translated_text: O steadfast one! You alone possess the skill to ferry the three worlds across to the far shore of the ocean of birth.

children.text: ko vā vihāya bhuvena kuhanāvarāhaṃ kṣoṇīsamuddhṛtividhau kuśalaḥ payodheḥ // 2.48 //
children.translated_text: Who, forsaking the cosmic boar, is able to lift the earth from the ocean? [2.48]
Having heard with respect this hymn composed by the gods,
the king of <s>Tuṣita</s> (the contented heaven), his heart delighted, replied to them in a voice deep as a rumbling thundercloud, with sweet syllables: [2.49]

children.text: bho bhoḥpurandaramukhā haridantapālāḥ sambhūya yūyamiha sādaramāgatāḥ kim /
children.translated_text: "Ho! <s>Purandara</s> (Indra) and others, guardians of <s>Hari</s>'s (Viṣṇu's) teeth (the directions), you have come together here with respect — why?

children.text: kārya mayā kimapi ced bhavatāmabhīṣṭa māvedyatāmalamiha stutisampadeti // 2.50 //
children.translated_text: If there is something I should do, some desire of yours, let it be made known — enough of this abundance of praise!" [2.50]

children.text: te 'pi prasannamanasaḥ praṇipatya tasmai vyajñāpayan vinayanamritapūrvakāyāḥ /
children.translated_text: They too, with gladdened minds, prostrating before him, announced with bodies bent in humility and voices preceded by nectar-like courtesy:
"O god of gods! The appropriate time has arrived for the awakening of the worlds!" [2.51]
Hearing those unprecedented words of theirs, he became absorbed in contemplation of the time and other factors for a moment,

children.text: niścitya tat sakalameva nidhirguṇānāṃ pratyabravīt punaramūn prathitāpadānaḥ // 2.52 //
children.translated_text: and then, having determined all that, that treasure of virtues of renowned deeds spoke again to them: [2.52]

children.text: śuddhodanasya sutatāmahametya satyaṃ sambodhanaṃ trijagatāṃ niyataṃ kariṣye /
children.translated_text: "Having truly become the son of <s>Śuddhodana</s>, I shall certainly bring about the awakening of the three worlds.
With my limbs, my wealth, and my very life-breath, it is for this alone that I previously accumulated this mass of merit." [2.53]

children.text: iti kṛtavati tasmin satyasandhe pratijñāṃ parahitaparabhāve pāramīpāraniṣṭhe /
children.translated_text: When that truthful one, who had reached the far shore of the <s>pāramīs</s> (perfections), devoted to the welfare of others, had made this vow,
they, with delighted minds, their bodies bristling with dense horripilation, departed as they wished. [2.54]

children.text: atha kānicideva vāsarāṇi kṣapayitvā tridive sa devarājaḥ /
children.translated_text: Then, having spent but a few days in heaven, that king of the gods
took conception in the chief queen of the king, who was resplendent with various vows. [2.55]

body.text: iti buddhaghoṣaviracite padyacūḍāmaṇināmni mahākāvye dvitīyaḥ sargaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the second canto of the <s>Padyacūḍāmaṇi</s> (Crown Jewel of Verse), a <s>mahākāvya</s> (great poem) composed by <s>Buddhaghoṣa</s>.
Third Canto: The Manifestation of the Signs of Pregnancy.

children.translated_text: Then that noble lady bore the signs of pregnancy, which were the dawn for the dynasty of <s>Śākya</s> kings,
a garland of joy for the eyes of the people, and a reassurance for the hearts of the virtuous. [3.1]

children.text: vivardhamānena ca madhyamena śyāmāyamānena ca cūcukena /
children.translated_text: By the swelling of her waist and by the darkening of her nipples,
the growth of the embryo in that doe-eyed woman became known to her friends through inference. [3.2]
When the <s>Bodhisattva</s> (the being destined for awakening), worthy of honor even to great sages, was in her womb,

children.text: madhyastadīyo manaso 'pi sūkṣmaḥ priyādiva sphītataro babhūva // 3.3 //
children.translated_text: her waist, subtle even to the mind, became fuller, like a beloved. [3.3]

children.text: yathā yathā vṛddhimavāpa tasyā madhyaṃ mahiṣyā mahanīyamūrtteḥ /
children.translated_text: As the waist of that queen of noble form grew and grew,
so too grew the body of her husband, who had been emaciated by grief at childlessness. [3.4]
The tips of her two breasts became discolored, together with the face of her co-wife.

children.text: kiñcānanaṃ garbhabharālasāyāḥ kīrttyā samaṃ pāṇḍuramāsa bharttuḥ // 3.5 //
children.translated_text: And the face of her, languid with the weight of pregnancy, became pale, along with the fame of her husband. [3.5]
Of the one within her, of wondrous prowess and a form that amazes all three worlds,
her breasts became dark-tipped, like masses of incense-smoke from the fire of his valor. [3.6]
The pair of breasts of that woman of faultless limbs, dark at the tips and pale in the remainder,
bore the beauty of the frontal lobes of the king of elephants, marked with mud from striking the river banks. [3.7]
Elder women performed protective rites for the son dwelling in the womb with various herbs;
and she herself became the protection of the three worlds from the afflictions caused by <s>Smara</s> (the god of love). [3.8]
At an auspicious hour, the king, fortunate like the spring that brings blossoms,

children.text: yathākramaṃ puṃsavanādi kṛtyaṃ nirvartayāmāsa nṛpo mahiṣyāḥ // 3.9 //
children.translated_text: duly performed the <s>puṃsavana</s> (male-child ceremony) and other rites for his queen heavy with the noble child. [3.9]
Like the dawn bringing forth the thousand-rayed sun, like the beauty of twilight bringing forth the cool-rayed moon,

children.text: bhadre muhūrte nṛpadharmapatnī prāsūta putraṃ bhuvanaikanetram // 3.10 //
children.translated_text: at an auspicious hour the queen gave birth to a son, the sole guide of the world. [3.10]
At that time, the earth, covered with magnificent lotuses,

children.text: sañchāditā tasya vihārahetoḥ kṛtopahāreva babhūva pṛthvī // 3.11 //
children.translated_text: raised up and decorated with five colors, appeared as if making an offering for his enjoyment. [3.11]
On branch after branch, with variegated petals and hundreds of blooming flowers,

children.text: cakāśire tasya vilokanāya sañjātanetrā iva śākhino 'pi // 3.12 //
children.translated_text: the trees shone as if they too had grown eyes to behold him. [3.12]
As if to show that the sprouting of <s>Buddha</s>-seeds on this earth is as rare as our own birth,
lotuses appeared on dry land as well as from the sky, for the viewing of embodied beings. [3.13]
By his teaching, the entire world of the living will truly attain <s>nirvāṇa</s> (liberation);
what wonder then that even the fires of hell were extinguished by his radiant splendor? [3.14]
Unable to bear the footsteps of that great soul, heavy as the fall of a mountain,
the earth trembled violently, its mountain bonds loosened. [3.15]

body.translated_text: Streams of water, tall as palm trees, suddenly burst through the earth and rose up,
as if the serpent world, subject to <s>Śeṣa</s>, had come to pay homage to that blessed soul. [3.16]

children.translated_text: By his streams of fame, spreading everywhere, pure as the waters of the heavenly river,
all the directions were being inscribed and became radiant. [3.17]

children.text: æjātaḥ pṛthivyāmadhipo munīnāmÆ iti bruvāṇā iva viṣṭapānām /
children.translated_text: As if proclaiming 'The lord of sages is born on earth!',
auspicious conch-shells, kettledrums, <s>mardala</s> (drums), and other varieties of instruments sounded of their own accord. [3.18]
As if engaged in performing the great consecration of that one of mighty influence,
all the oceans surged beyond their bounds, their waves rising high with laughter. [3.19]
The one called 'Immovable' — <s>Meru</s> — trembled; the report of the salt ocean — the sea — faltered;
the name 'flowing' of the river was belied as it ceased to flow; the epithet 'stable' of the earth was overthrown. [3.20]
The cloud, deep-voiced as the ocean, rained even without the rainy season;
such wondrous deeds occurred when the prince, foremost of the good, was born. [3.21]
With the sound of many beaten <s>mṛdaṅgas</s> (drums) making the mouths of the caves of the horizons resound,
with the mountains shaking from the whirling of joyous dancing that rocked the earth,
with the grounds bejeweled by pearls from necklaces shattered by mutual embracing,
with all the quarters adorned by handfuls of thrown powder and ground sandalwood,
with ornaments flung at one another and diadems and crest-jewels scattered,
the splendor of that birth-festival was as if the three worlds were a single household. [3.24]
The mother shone even more with her son, whose complexion was rosy with the freshness of a newborn,
like the shore with the young moon, whose form is red at its new rising. [3.25]
By the splendor of his body, blazing like heated gold and spreading forth,
the lamps in the birthing chamber became like stars at dawn. [3.26]
Hearing the exceedingly wondrous news of his son's birth from the women of the inner chambers, the king
became stupefied, his mental functions overwhelmed by a swoon of joy, not knowing what to do. [3.27]
Not having seen in the three worlds anything worthy of being given as a gift for this,
nevertheless, that exceedingly generous king honored him with the giving of all his possessions. [3.28]

children.text: bhadre muhūrte sa patiḥ prajānāṃ dadarśa devyāḥ stimitāyatākṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: At an auspicious moment, that lord of the people gazed with wide, motionless eyes at the prince

children.text: kumāramutsaṅgatale śayānaṃ taṭe taṭinyā iva haṃsaśāvam // 3.29 //
children.translated_text: lying in the lap of the queen — like a swan-chick on the bank of a river. [3.29]
For the father who was savoring with unwearied, thirsty eyes the moon-face of his son,
there was no restraining the flood of tears of joy that arose in his body bristling with horripilation. [3.30]
Having drunk deeply with the cupped hands of his eyes the moon-disk face of the suckling infant,
an inexhaustible treasury of boundless beauty, the king of kings attained supreme contentment. [3.31]
Having completed through the family priest the <s>jātakarma</s> (birth rite) and other exceedingly grand ceremonies for his son,
he gave him the name '<s>Siddhārtha</s>' (one whose aims are fulfilled) — praised by the world and fitting for no other. [3.32]
As the sky is adorned by a new raincloud, as the night by a new moon,
as a great forest by a lion cub, so was the dynasty adorned by him. [3.33]
The king was as delighted by his indistinct baby words

children.text: tathā na gānairapi gāyakānāṃ mahākavīnāmapi vāgvilāsaiḥ // 3.34 //
children.translated_text: as he was not by the songs of singers or the verbal artistry of great poets. [3.34]
His face, naturally fragrant and utterly charming, of such delicacy,
became the common, ever-fresh play-lotus of the beauties of the inner chambers. [3.35]
With the mind-delighting and resonant tinkling of jeweled anklets, [bringing] delight to his mother,
the little son played on jeweled floors, as if coaxing his own reflection with affection. [3.36]
As the young child played in the dust with the trusted sons of ministers,

children.text: saṃgrāmabhūdhūliṣu bhāvinīṣu svairaṃ vihartuṃ vihiteva yogyā // 3.37 //
children.translated_text: it was as if a rehearsal was being freely conducted for the dust of future battlefields. [3.37]
That prince, playing boldly with the lion-cubs of the inner chambers, along with the other royal sons,
long maintained what was like a training in his own wondrous prowess for them. [3.38]
The royal swans of the palace, drawn by the delightful sound of his jeweled bells,

children.text: tatāṭa pādena tadīyarājaśabdāsahiṣṇuḥ kila tān kumāraḥ // 3.39 //
children.translated_text: the prince kicked with his foot, for he could not bear the royal title (<s>rāja</s>) being applied to them. [3.39]
With his head tossed by the blow of nail-scratches, with the glory of his trumpeting streaming from his mouth,
with a line of auspicious <s>mada</s> (rut-fluid) flowing forth, the young child enacted the play of a rut-elephant. [3.40]
Radiant with a garland of gleaming <s>campaka</s> flowers, illuminating the world of the living with his luster,

children.text: sa dārako dīpa iva pradīptaḥ śokāndhakāraṃ vinināya pitroḥ // 3.41 //
children.translated_text: that child, like a blazing lamp, dispelled the darkness of sorrow from his parents. [3.41]
Having received the sacred thread, his earliest childhood now past, for the thorough study of all branches of knowledge
The lord of the earth entrusted the best of princes into the hands of the teachers. // 3.42 //

children.text: sa deśikendrairupadiśyamānā vidyāḥ samastāḥ sakalāḥ kalāśca /
children.translated_text: All the sciences and all the arts, as taught by the foremost of instructors,
he grasped quickly through his keen intellect, as a mass of rain-clouds [grasps] the waters of the ocean. // 3.43 //
The sciences, having found a prince of incomparable intelligence, shone forth all the more,
like the garlands of moonbeams of the lord of stars [i.e., the Moon] upon the clear expanse of the autumn sky. // 3.44 //

children.text: nitāntamānandayatā prajānāṃ manāṃsi sadyo haratā tamāṃsi /
children.translated_text: With one who exceedingly delighted the minds of the people and instantly dispelled their darkness,
the <s>Śākya</s> lineage surged with splendor through him, like the great ocean at the rising of the moon. // 3.45 //

children.text: prabheva bhānoḥ pratibheva sūreḥ śikheva dīpasya dayeva sādhoḥ /
children.translated_text: Like the radiance of the sun, like the brilliance of a hero, like the flame of a lamp, like the compassion of a saint,
like the moonlight of the moon, like the nectar of the ocean — thus arose his beauty of new youth. // 3.46 //
As if sharpened on the whetstone of youthful splendor by <s>Manobhava</s> (the god of love),
his limbs, with their marks made manifest and joints well-proportioned, became [resplendent]. // 3.47 //
That pair of his feet, beautiful by nature, marked with lines of a thousand spokes and the sign of the wheel,
verily mocked the fresh lotus groves with the moonlight of their nail-radiance. // 3.48 //
The prince, whose waist was lovely, adorned with three folds, and tightly set,
appeared like Mount <s>Manthāra</s> (the churning mountain) encircled by the coils of <s>Vāsuki</s>, with its radiant middle. // 3.49 //
The roundness of the prince's hips attained fullness along with all his virtues,
while the region of his waist attained slenderness along with [the diminishing of] all his faults. // 3.50 //
The pool of his navel, like a pit fashioned by <s>Manobhava</s> (the god of love) seeking to plant
a blue staff of a banner in the form of the line of hair, appeared on the prince's [body]. // 3.51 //
As if to give unrestricted space to <s>Śrī</s> (the goddess of beauty), who was uncomfortable within the lotus,
the space between the arms of that prince of meritorious nature became as vast as the rock-surface of the <s>Vindhya</s> mountain. // 3.52 //
Since the chest of that valorous prince was as hard as a diamond door-panel,

children.text: cakruḥ kavāṭaṃ sadaneṣu sattvā vibhūṣaṇārthaṃ na tu rakṣaṇārtham // 3.53 //
children.translated_text: beings made door-panels in their homes merely for adornment, not for protection. // 3.53 //
His arm, long as the body of the lord of serpents, belonging to one skilled in protecting the people,
became a barrier for the protection of the three worlds, making rival kings tremble. // 3.54 //
His neck, with its beautifully curved form, with most distinctly visible lines,
appeared as if [adorned] with the seal-marks of armlets that tightly and lovingly embraced the beauty of his splendor. // 3.55 //

children.text: mugdhasya tasyāsa mukhāmbujasya mahotpalasyāpi mahān viśeṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: Between his charming lotus-face and the great blue lotus, there was a great distinction:

children.text: vāṇimalolāṃ vahati sma pūrvaṃ svabhāvalolāmitaratu lakṣmīm // 3.56 //
children.translated_text: the former bore <s>Vāṇī</s> (<s>Sarasvatī</s>), who is fickle [in her speech]; the latter bore <s>Lakṣmī</s>, who is fickle by nature. // 3.56 //

children.text: vāṇyā vareṇyasya mukhe vasantyā mañjīraśiñjānamivāsa sūktam /
children.translated_text: With <s>Vāṇī</s> (the goddess of speech) dwelling in the mouth of that excellent one, beautiful speech was like the tinkling of anklet-bells;
the splendor of his smile was like his nail-radiance, and his row of teeth was like a rosary of pearls. // 3.57 //
By the beauty and splendor of that lotus-face, his cheek-surface [had] the beauty of a jewel-mirror;
his ear-ornament was a swing of grace, and his eye was a pool of playfulness. // 3.58 //
The creeper-like eyebrow of that one of captivating form, with both tips licked by starlight,
was like the playful bow [of <s>Kāma</s>] that, having conquered <s>Māra</s>, had claimed as its own the string threaded with black bees. // 3.59 //
His lotus-like face, charming with the beautiful circle of the <s>ūrṇā</s> (auspicious mark), radiant with light,
extended the beauty of the orb of the rising sun, mostly [concealing] the crescent moon within. // 3.60 //
The forehead of the prince, lovely with the <s>ūrṇā</s>, shone exceedingly,
like the rocky plateau of Mount <s>Meru</s> with the sprouting tusks of elephants concealed within, broken by rampart-like action. // 3.61 //
Without rouge, without armlets, without ear-ornaments, and even without garlands,
his body, by new youth alone, manifested a beauty that was irresistibly captivating. // 3.62 //
Delighting the doe-eyed women, [yet] without a lustful gaze toward other men's [wives],
the collective beauty of his entire body arose as an artless ornament. // 3.63 //
For the son whose arms were fit to bear the bracelet of the earth, the king, of a nature rivaling <s>Indra</s>,
performed the consecration as crown prince (<s>yuvarāja</s>) with waters purified by jewels and <s>mantras</s>, from ruby-filled golden vessels and sacred waters. // 3.64 //

body.text: iti buddhaghoṣaviracite padyacūḍāmaṇināmni mahākāvye tṛtīyaḥ sargaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the third canto in the <s>mahākāvya</s> called <s>Padyacūḍāmaṇi</s>, composed by <s>Buddhaghoṣa</s>.
Fourth Canto: The Proposal for <s>Siddhārtha</s>'s Marriage

children.text: atho kumārasya kulodvahasya karagrahaṃ kārayituṃ narendraḥ /
children.translated_text: Then, in order to arrange the hand-taking [marriage] of the prince, the upholder of his lineage,

children.text: kā sāsya yogyā bhuvi kanyaketi cintayāmāsa sametabandhuḥ // 4.1 //
children.translated_text: the king, together with his kinsmen, pondered: 'Which maiden on earth is worthy of him?' // 4.1 //
Meanwhile, the <s>Koliya</s> king [sent word]: 'I shall give my princess, the jewel-lamp of the family,

children.text: dāsyāmi sūnostava sarvatheti sandeśapatraṃ visasarja tasmai // 4.2 //
children.translated_text: to your son in every way' — and dispatched a letter of this message to him. // 4.2 //
Having heard the news from the mouth of the messenger, the king, his mind exceedingly delighted,

children.text: tathaiva sajjīkriyatāṃ tvayeti sandeśamasmai prajighāya bhūyaḥ // 4.3 //
children.translated_text: sent back to him the further message: 'Let it be prepared accordingly.' // 4.3 //

children.text: tatheti so 'pi pratigṛhya tasmai sandeśapatraṃ samudīrṇaharṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: He too, accepting the letter with overflowing joy and [saying] 'So be it,'
commenced preparing the grand festive ceremony of the princess's marriage-consecration (<s>vivāhadīkṣā</s>). // 4.4 //
With rows of banners erected to touch the clouds, with the beauty of silk canopies fastened [above],
with the mark of towering rainbow-colored arches, and with full pitchers placed within,
with the ground made lovely by strewn pearl-sand, scattered with offerings of various flowers,
the inner apartments of the king assumed the arrangement of the wedding preparations. // 4.6 //
With the [bride's] body anointed with fragrant oil and smeared with spotless yellow unguent,
the noble women reverently bathed her with [waters poured from] jeweled golden vessels, [like] rain-clouds [pouring water]. // 4.7 //
At the conclusion of the bath, the princess, removing the garment wet with water,

children.text: samādade cārutaraṃ dukūlaṃ candrātapaṃ śāradikeva rātriḥ // 4.8 //
children.translated_text: took up a more beautiful silk cloth, like an autumn night [taking up] the moonlight as a sunshade. // 4.8 //
Then, having seated her in the center of a pavilion strewn with fresh blossoms, her companions,
most skillful, adorned the king's daughter with ornaments of various kinds. // 4.9 //
The hair-arrangement with fresh <s>mallī</s> (jasmine) woven within, upon her of restless eyes,
extended the beauty of a thick cluster of darkness studded with multitudes of stars. // 4.10 //
With excellent curling locks, her lotus-face appeared
as if [surrounded by] black bees clinging [to it], drawn by the abundance of its fragrance. // 4.11 //
The wedding-consecration mark (<s>tilaka</s>) on the princess's [forehead], fashioned with vermillion, shone,
like a blazing sun of the glory of <s>Manobhava</s> (the god of love) who had attained sovereignty, about to rise. // 4.12 //
The barley-sprouts attached to the ears of the lotus-eyed maiden shone exceedingly,
as if [they were] the sprouting fame of the flower-armed [<s>Kāma</s>], conqueror of the three worlds, spreading forth. // 4.13 //
Her cheek, with its leaf-pattern drawn in musk, having the beauty of the moon's orb,
stood surpassing the beauty of a mirror whose interior is soiled by the winds of clouds. // 4.14 //
The eye of the fish-eyed maiden, made beautiful with applied black collyrium,
rivaled the beauty of <s>Anaṅga</s>'s (the bodiless Kāma's) arrow, smeared with the mud of the most terrible <s>hālāhala</s> poison. // 4.15 //
Of her charming lip, which was incomparably rosy [by nature],
the applied coating of lac-dye did not produce a beauty that had not existed before. // 4.16 //
Her face, adorned with pearl earrings and bearing a gentle smile,
surpassed an autumn lotus flanked on both sides by lotus-bud sheaths. // 4.17 //
Wearing a pearl necklace beautiful to behold upon her neck, she shone exceedingly,
like a wave of the ocean, radiant with a conch that has cast forth heaps of pearls. // 4.18 //
Her body, anointed with sandal paste and decorated with patterns of fragrant <s>agaru</s> (aloe),
nurtured the beauty of the heavenly <s>Gaṅgā</s>, whose intervals are variegated by the [waters of the] <s>Yamunā</s>. // 4.19 //
The pair of her breasts, of that woman of faultless limbs, bearing a glistening pearl necklace,
took on the beauty of the peak of the western mountain, adorned with scatterings of multitudes of stars. // 4.20 //
Slender, her waist adorned with three folds, bearing a swaying necklace upon her breasts,
she shone like the <s>Gaṅgā</s> with its waves, its body sprinkled with spray, and bearing <s>cakravāka</s> birds. // 4.21 //
The king's daughter, her hips weighted with a girdle strung with rubies,
[was] like the earth, jewel-bearing at its ocean-shore, embraced by the sandy coast. // 4.22 //
The new line of hair on her body shone, ascending the high mountain of her breasts,
like a suspended garland of blue lotuses, [hung] for the purpose of supporting the source of erotic love (<s>śṛṅgāra</s>). // 4.23 //
The slender-bodied one shone with ornaments fashioned of priceless gold,
like a moving <s>campaka</s> creeper, resplendent with fresh flower-clusters. // 4.24 //
The pair of her feet, their redness enhanced by the touch of lac-dye, soft, belonging to the large-eyed one,
humbled the beauty of lotuses visible in the special touch of the morning sun. // 4.25 //
As if wishing to see the beauty of her full adornment, she, holding a crystal hand-mirror,
shone like the [autumnal] direction with a clear sky, in contact with the full moon's orb. // 4.26 //
Then, upon the graceful-bodied one whose wishes were fully realized, the priests

children.text: na kevalaṃ kautukamābabandhuḥ karāmbuje kiñca hadambuje 'pi // 4.27 //
children.translated_text: tied the auspicious thread not only on her lotus-like hand, but also on her lotus-like heart. // 4.27 //
Having thus completed the wedding-adornment preparation of the princess,
the <s>Koliya</s> king, filled with eager anticipation, stood watching for the arrival of the bridegroom. // 4.28 //
Meanwhile, in his own palace, the chief prince, bathed, anointed, and clad in freshly washed garments,
put on the wedding ornaments that were a feast for the eyes of the world. // 4.29 //
In a fine linen upper garment interwoven with gold thread, the prince
shone like the expanse of the sky with an autumn cloud enveloped by lightning. // 4.30 //
The prince was radiant with a string of pearls hanging upon his broad chest,
like Mount <s>Meru</s>, golden, with a reflected path [of light] along its slopes. // 4.31 //
The prince, of serene and majestic form, with earrings of coral, pearl, and crystal,
[was] adorned like Mount <s>Meru</s> with the orbs of the blazing sun and the lord of stars [the moon]. // 4.32 //
The bridegroom shone, moist with <s>Haricandana</s> (divine sandal-paste), like the eastern mountain reddened by the morning sun,
like an elephant dappled with streaks of mineral ore, like the nectar-rayed [moon] dense with twilight glow. // 4.33 //
In the surface of a mirror, the reflected body of the youth adorned with jeweled ornaments

children.text: vaikartanaṃ maṇḍalamāsthitasya puṃsaḥ purāṇasya pupoṣa lakṣmīm // 4.34 //
children.translated_text: nurtured the beauty of the Primeval Person (<s>Puruṣa</s>) established in the solar orb. // 4.34 //
The innate radiance of the prince's body surpassed [any] artificial adornment;
the other ruby ornaments became merely signs of sovereignty. // 4.35 //
With the beauty of a raised pearl parasol and attended by waving white yak-tail fans,
having mounted the wedding vehicle, the prince proceeded to the house of his bride's family. // 4.36 //
The <s>Koliya</s> king, [seeing] that lamp of the <s>Śākya</s> lineage arriving,
himself went far on foot to receive him and led him to the wedding pavilion. // 4.37 //

children.text: dadarśa dhīraḥ kṣitipālaputrīṃ tatra sthitāṃ tārakarājavaktrām /
children.translated_text: The steadfast [prince] there beheld the king's daughter, standing, her face like the lord of stars,
shining as if she were a daughter of the ocean, with a playful lotus in her hand. // 4.38 //
As the prince gazed with longing at the maiden whose body mocked the beauty of the nectar-rayed [moon],
the ocean of his joy, surpassing its bounds, spread far. // 4.39 //

children.text: yat kāryate tatra pativratābhiḥ kṛtvā tadetat sakalaṃ kumāraḥ /
children.translated_text: Having performed all that is done there by devoted wives, the prince
together with her of lotus-wide eyes, entered the center of the ritual altar. // 4.40 //
Before that brightly flaming sacrificial fire, blazing high with oblations,
the priest, skilled in the ritual procedure, joined the bride and groom. || 4.41 ||
The prince's body-staff was clad in a coat of erect goosebumps;
the stamens fallen from the garland across his chest seemed to serve as guardians of that treasure of virtues. || 4.42 ||
The <s>Koliya</s> maiden's fingers were moist with tiny drops of perspiration;
these served as the sprinkled droplets of the wedding water-ceremony for the wide-eyed one. || 4.43 ||
Advancing out of eagerness to behold, and retreating again out of modesty,
their sidelong glances at that time bore the beauty of a swing's playful movement. || 4.44 ||
As if practicing the whirling play of the eddy-wheel of the wedding-circumambulation waters,
the groom, together with the doe-eyed one, performed the clockwise circumambulation of the fire. || 4.45 ||
The wedding fire, beholding the bride and groom of captivating beauty, never before seen,
on the pretext of the flickering of its clockwise flames, seemed to perform a nod of the head in admiration. || 4.46 ||

children.text: guruprayuktā kulapālikā sā lājopahāra visasarja vahnau /
children.translated_text: The family matriarch, directed by the elders, offered parched rice into the fire—
like a vine in a mango grove of newly sprouted shoots, releasing its flowers when shaken by the wind. || 4.47 ||
The rising mass of smoke from the fire, clinging near her moon-like face,
acted as an unfading dark-blue lotus-stalk pattern for the lotus-eyed one. || 4.48 ||
The line of fresh smoke that rose from it, on her face that was pleased to receive it,
was seen moving for a moment like a garland of bees on a lotus. || 4.49 ||
The auspicious smoke-line, scattered around the lotus-face of the beautiful-browed one,
bestowed the actual beauty of a halo, as of another wandering moon. || 4.50 ||
The wedding line of auspicious smoke, encircling the lotus-face of the beautiful-eyed one,
bore the beauty of a momentary face-veil fashioned of a dark-blue cloth. || 4.51 ||
The lotus-face of the doe-eyed one, upon receiving the smoke, had eyes narrowed from the sting of collyrium-like vapors,
cheek-petals distressed by the holy water, and ear-lotuses faded. || 4.52 ||
Thus, step by step, having had his hand pressed in marriage, the prince, together with her,
bowed to his parents-in-law, and they, approving, nourished these two with blessings. || 4.53 ||

children.text: anyāṃśca sarvānapi bandhuvargān sambhāvya jāyāsahitaḥ kumāraḥ /
children.translated_text: Having honored all the other groups of relatives as well, the prince, accompanied by his wife,
went forth from there, the best of men, for the circumambulation of his own capital. || 4.54 ||
At that moment, the women of <s>Kapilavastu</s>, intent on gazing at the prince—
on every mansion, amorous gestures instructed by <s>Madana</s> (the god of love) arose. || 4.55 ||
For one, holding a garland of white lotuses with her tender hand,

children.text: svayaṃ varītuṃ kila rājadhānīsopānamārgaṃ tvarayā jagāma // 4.56 //
children.translated_text: hurried down the stairway of the royal capital, as if to choose a bridegroom herself. || 4.56 ||

children.text: netrasya taddarśananiścalasya mā mūdidaṃ rodha itīva matvā /
children.translated_text: 'Let not this obstruction be the ruin of my eye, fixed without blinking at the sight of him'—thinking thus,
one long-eyed woman quickly pushed aside the collyrium [screen] and reached the window. || 4.57 ||

children.text: vibhūṣaṇairantarite madaṅge naisargikīṃ kāntimasau na paśyet /
children.translated_text: 'With ornaments obstructing my limbs, he will not see my natural beauty'—

children.text: itīva naipathyamakalpayantī kācit prapede sahasā gavākṣam // 4.58 //
children.translated_text: thinking thus, as if removing her costume, one suddenly reached the lattice-window. || 4.58 ||

children.text: vyākośametad yadi karṇapāśe niveśayeyaṃ surabhi dvirephaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'If I place this fragrant, fully-opened [flower] at my ear, a bee

children.text: māṃ pīḍayedityavadhīrya manye karṇotpalaṃ kāpi jagāma jālam // 4.59 //
children.translated_text: will torment me'—disdaining [the flower], one, I think, went to the lattice, abandoning her ear-lotus. || 4.59 ||
'The goosebumps on my breast, arising from the joy of beholding his face, are themselves the ornament'—
thinking thus, as if discarding her breast-ornament of painted leaves, one reached the vicinity of the window. || 4.60 ||

children.text: pativratāyāḥ paradarśanāya yātrā na yukteti nirundhatīva /
children.translated_text: 'The journey of a faithful wife to behold another man is not proper'—as if restraining her,
the girdle slipping from one woman's ample hips clasped her ankle. || 4.61 ||
One, not having placed her single-strand necklace (<s>ekāvalī</s>) from neck to neck, but carrying it
in her lotus-like hand, with eager mind, set forth as if to offer it to him as a gift. || 4.62 ||
With those women, devoted to gazing up at him, the terraces of the mansions,
without interval, became like an army encampment of <s>Makaradhvaja</s> (Kāma), who desires to conquer the world. || 4.63 ||
In every street, the trembling sidelong glances of the alluring women fell upon him—
like the flower-arrows of the Flower-bannered One (<s>Kāma</s>), whose body was hidden behind the palace lattices. || 4.64 ||
Those long-eyed women gazed at him with sidelong glances stretched to their ears,
unable to pass from one limb to another of his enviable body, never sated. || 4.65 ||
The prince, with their lotus-friend-like eyes, unblinking with wonder,

children.text: aṅgeṣu sarvatra niṣiktabimbaiḥ sākṣāt sahasrākṣa ivābabhāse // 4.66 //
children.translated_text: their reflections cast upon every part of his body, appeared verily like a thousand-eyed <s>Indra</s>. || 4.66 ||
Wherever the women directed their gaze upon the prince's body,
there beauty remained adhering, as if exuded and sewn in. || 4.67 ||
The prince's form, entering the heart of each of those smitten women,
with eyes wide and motionless, seemed to wish to cure the affliction of love. || 4.68 ||
One woman, her body-staff bristling with goosebumps, her eyes closed in ecstasy,
smelled a lotus held in her hand, which was indistinguishable from his lotus-face. || 4.69 ||
One, as if wishing to recite an attraction-spell taught by <s>Kāma</s>,
slowly turned in her hand a necklace-strand as if it were a rosary of pearls. || 4.70 ||
One, with a nail as pink as a parrot's beak-cup, was inscribing upon
a fresh <s>ketaka</s> petal held in her hand, as if to compose a love-letter for him. || 4.71 ||
One, holding in her tender hand a drawing-board with a brush,

children.text: ātmānamālikhya varāya tasmai dātuṃ samudyogavatīva tasthau // 4.72 //
children.translated_text: stood as if intent on drawing herself and giving it to that groom. || 4.72 ||
Under the incessant shower of pollen from the flower-arrows of the Mind-born (<s>Kāma</s>),
the gaze of one woman seemed to be clouded, overflowing with copious tears. || 4.73 ||
The cheek-line of one woman shone beautifully with sprouting goosebumps,
like an auspicious vessel with growing shoots at the entry of the Mind-born (<s>Kāma</s>) into the mansion of the heart. || 4.74 ||
Shaken as if by the wind from the wings of <s>Kāma's</s> row of arrow-volleys
drawn to the ear, one woman trembled, her upper garment slipping. || 4.75 ||
One, sprinkled with the drops of holy water that had arisen,
shone like a bow-vine of <s>Smara</s> (Kāma), firmly drawn, sprouting with discharged pearl-buds. || 4.76 ||
As the Mind-born entered her mental avenue, with the scattered dust of his footsteps,

children.text: kācid dṛśaṃ karburavigraheva vivarṇabhāvaṃ pratipadyate sma // 4.77 //
children.translated_text: one woman's gaze, as if her body were speckled, took on a discolored hue. || 4.77 ||
'What immeasurable merit did this ruby-lipped one perform in previous births
to obtain this prince, the chief of the mountain of her family, as her husband, so supremely handsome?' || 4.78 ||
'The Creator, in first making the moon-orb, that storehouse of nectar, and the lotuses, those chariots of <s>Lakṣmī</s>,
was, as it were, rehearsing for the creation of his face.' || 4.79 ||
'The Lotus-born (<s>Brahmā</s>), having gathered and gathered the essence of beauty
during the creation of the three worlds and then bestowing it, seems to have made this one the crown prince.' || 4.80 ||
'To behold this youth, with arms long as a yoke, whose beauty is coveted by the three worlds—
why did <s>Viriñci</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>), the knower of the three worlds, not give our eyes ten thousand [instead of two]?' || 4.81 ||
'From partaking of the nectar of beauty born from the nectar-moon-disc of his face,
whose pair of eyes does not attain the state of unblinking in this very birth?' || 4.82 ||
Hearing such supremely generous words of these women, pleasing to the ear,
the prince, having circumambulated the city, entered the inner palace of the king. || 4.83 ||
Entering with his head deeply bowed, his palms joined in the bud of salutation,

children.text: tayā sametaḥ śakavaṃśadīpaḥ priyottaraṅgaṃ pitaraṃ vavande // 4.184 //
children.translated_text: the lamp of the <s>Śākya</s> lineage, together with her, saluted his father, who surged with delight. || 4.84 ||
Raising up his deeply-bowing son together with his bride, with both arms forming a cage,
the king, his body-staff covered with goosebumps, embraced him respectfully. || 4.85 ||
Then the women of the retinue, with camphor lamps placed in golden vessels,
performed the auspicious <s>nīrājana</s> (lamp-waving) ceremony for him as he was seated on the throne. || 4.83 ||
Beholding the prince, whose marriage was thus performed, whose fame spread through the world,

children.text: narapatiravalokya prīyamāṇaḥ sa mene nijakulamatituṅgaṃ nihanutārātigarvam // 4.187 //
children.translated_text: who had girded himself with the vow of protecting the three worlds—the king, delighting, considered his own lineage supremely exalted and the pride of his enemies crushed. || 4.87 ||

body.text: iti buddhaghoṣaviracite padyacūḍāmaṇināmni mahākāvye caturthaḥ sargaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the fourth canto of the <s>Mahākāvya</s> called <s>Padyacūḍāmaṇi</s>, composed by <s>Buddhaghoṣa</s>.
Fifth Canto: The Three Great Palaces

children.translated_text: Then the king, of complete splendor, for the prince in the bloom of new youth,
had three incomparable great palaces built, suitable for the celebration of the festivals of the seasons. || 5.1 ||
In those mansions, the prince, son of the chief of kings,
diverted himself with the enchanting playful dances of the finest courtesans, rich in varied artful arrangements. || 5.2 ||
Then the rainy season arrived—industrious in pacifying the fever of the harsh summer upon the earth,
the supreme teacher of the steps of the graceful dance performed by the circles of peacocks in every forest. || 5.3 ||
Certain clouds, dark as glass, blown by violent winds, shone forth—
as if old skins gradually shed by the dark serpent of the sky. || 5.4 ||

children.text: tadā samāruhya vihāramaṇḍapaṃ sahaiva vadhvā sarasīruhekṣaṇaḥ /
children.translated_text: Then, ascending the pleasure-pavilion together with his bride, the lotus-eyed prince,

children.text: pradarśayan mīnadṛśaḥ payodharān pracakrame varṇayituṃ tapātyayam // 5.5 //
children.translated_text: showing the fish-eyed one the rain-clouds, began to describe the end of summer: || 5.5 ||
'Behold from here, O lotus-eyed one, the clouds—carrying away the burden of ocean-water,
resembling the disc of the earth entered into the mirror of the pleasure-sport of the sky-expanse! || 5.6 ||
With fresh fragments of rain-clouds, as if with collyrium-heaps

children.text: natabhru! navyaiḥ śakalaiḥ payomucāṃ nabhaḥsthalī pātramiyaṃ vibhāvyate // 5.7 //
children.translated_text: polished by the lamps of blazing lightning of the season's beauty—O arched-browed one, this sky appears as a cosmetic vessel! || 5.7 ||
As if the braids of the directions are being loosened upon reunion

children.text: vimucyamānā iva keśaveṇayo vibhānti kāmaṃ navameghapaṃktayaḥ // 5.8 //
children.translated_text: with the rainy season, a long-absent traveler—the rows of fresh clouds, O beloved, beautifully appear! || 5.8 ||
As if the smoke-waves of the summer-fire, born of the ritual hearth, subsiding

children.text: vijṛmbhamāṇā iva dhūmavīcayo viśanti meghāvalayo viyattalam // 5.9 //
children.translated_text: with the arrival of the end of heat, are expanding—the rows of clouds enter the sky-expanse. || 5.9 ||
The mountains, which formerly descended to the ocean with clipped wings out of fear of <s>Indra's</s> assault,
seem now to fly up again from there under the pretext of the new rain-clouds. || 5.10 ||
O doe-eyed one, the sky without interval shines with clouds reflected by the lightning-vine's hand,
like the ocean at the end of an age with coral-vine-tossed mud-balls! || 5.11 ||
Beholding the wondrous beauty of the peacocks' dance, sweet-voiced,

children.text: vilokya vidyunnayanena vibhramān praśaṃsatīva stanitena toyadaḥ // 5.12 //
children.translated_text: on the forest-stage, the rain-cloud seems to applaud with thunder, watching their movements with the eye of lightning. || 5.12 ||
The peacocks, grasping in their beaks the serpent-world-jewels resembling golden bangles,
cry out, filling the sky with deep calls, their tail-fans spread in circles. || 5.13 ||
As if gold streaks are being rubbed against the touchstone-slab of the row of cloud-surfaces
by the goldsmith that is the end-of-summer season—the lightning-vines gleam, O <s>Cakora</s>-eyed one! || 5.14 ||
Dark only is my outer body; but my inner heart is pure.

children.text: iti sphuraccañcaladīdhiticchalād vibhidya taṃ darśayatīva vāridaḥ // 5.15 //
children.translated_text: thus, by the pretext of its flickering, trembling radiance, the cloud seems to split it open and reveal [the sky]. [5.15]
Of the weighty [earth], which bears the ocean as its rim, situated in the midst of the four great oceans,

children.text: kūlādrikūṭeṣu taḍidgaṇāvṛtā vibhānti sītā iva meghapaṃktayaḥ // 5.16 //
children.translated_text: upon the peaks of the coastal mountains, the rows of clouds, enveloped in clusters of lightning, shine like white garlands. [5.16]
Having conquered the triple world by the wondrous splendor of their generous valor, by those clouds,

children.text: samucchritānāṃ taralākṣi! vidyuto jayadhvajānāṃ janayanti saṃśayam // 5.17 //
children.translated_text: O tremulous-eyed one! the lightnings create doubt [whether they are] the victory-banners of the lofty [clouds]. [5.17]
O restless-eyed one! the lightnings flash like cane-sticks used to wave white fly-whisks,
swaying like finger-branches wielded by the dense wealth-clouds in the act of threatening the departed. [5.18]
Playfully taking up the great bow of <s>Indra</s>, whose beautiful bowstring is fashioned from lightning,
the rainy season, like a <s>Śabara</s> (hunter), pierces the lotus-less earth with volleys of rain-arrows. [5.19]
The fireflies of <s>Puruhūta</s> (<s>Indra</s>) flash with the splendor of hood-gems disgorged by serpent-eaters,
their beauty like scattered fragments of jewels dislodged from gem-studded pillars struck by fierce torrents. [5.20]
On the fresh grassy ground, resembling the luminous expanse of an autumn night sky,
fall the fireflies of <s>Indra</s>'s thunderbolt, resembling red stars of the evening twilight. [5.21]

children.text: æviyatpṛthivyoḥ kiyadantaraṃ bhavetÆ iti pramātuṃ prathamena vedhasā /
children.translated_text: "How great would be the distance between sky and earth?" — as if to measure this, by the primordial Creator,

children.text: prasāryamāṇā iva mānarajjavaḥ patanti dhārāḥ paritaḥ payomucām // 5.22 //
children.translated_text: the streams of rain fall from the clouds on all sides, as if they were measuring ropes being stretched out. [5.22]
O <s>cakora</s>-eyed one! this garland of clouds, with its circle of abundantly chattering crane-hosts,
having taken up conch shells, seems to loudly proclaim the march of the Sugarcane-bowed one (<s>Kāmadeva</s>) at the face of the quarters. [5.23]
With necks graceful as the curves of crane-rows, wearing colorful blankets of <s>Indra</s>'s bow (rainbow),
the young cloud-elephants bow upon the mountains, as if lowered for the purpose of striking the slopes, bearing their thunderous roars. [5.24]
The directions, adorned with garlands of <s>campaka</s>-like momentary lightning, wearing beautiful crests of <s>Indra</s>'s rainbow,
seem to anoint one another with cloud-horns pregnant with fresh water. [5.25]
As the sovereign of the seasons, the conqueror of summer, enters the mansion of the sky,

children.text: ghanena baddhā iva toraṇasrajaḥ surendracāpāḥ sutarāṃ cakāsati // 5.26 //
children.translated_text: the rainbows shine most brilliantly, as if they were festoon-garlands tied to the gateway by the clouds. [5.26]
When the wall of the horizon is shaken playfully by the thunder-elephant scratching against it,

children.text: viśīryamāṇā iva tārakāgaṇāḥ palāṇḍubhāsaḥ karakāḥ patantyamūḥ // 5.27 //
children.translated_text: these onion-bright hailstones fall, as if clusters of stars were crumbling down. [5.27]

children.text: payaḥpravāhaiḥ samameva vāridaḥ paraṃ samādāya mahāpayonidheḥ /
children.translated_text: The cloud, having fully received [water] from the great ocean together with streams of water,

children.text: punarvibhaktā iva mauktikotkarāḥ sphuranti varṣopalaśarkarāḥ kṣitau // 5.28 //
children.translated_text: the hailstones glitter upon the earth, as if heaps of pearls were being redistributed. [5.28]
Just as the lightning-fire expands in the circle of clouds through the rains,

children.text: tathā tathā pānthamṛgīdṛśāṃ dhruvaṃ vijṛmbhate cetasi manmathānalaḥ // 5.29 //
children.translated_text: so too does the fire of <s>Manmatha</s> (Love) surely expand in the hearts of doe-eyed women whose husbands are traveling. [5.29]
The forest-ground, ablaze with summer's heat, stretching out its hand of blossoming <s>kandalī</s> flowers,
with the enchanting cries of peacock calls, seems to entreat the clouds for life. [5.30]
Bearing the pollen of flower-filaments from the blossoms of groves bowing in the awakened forest,

children.text: haranti mandāḥ pavamānakandalāḥ śikhaṇḍināṃ tāṇḍavajaṃ pariśramam // 5.31 //
children.translated_text: the gentle gusts of wind remove the fatigue born of the <s>tāṇḍava</s> dance of the peacocks. [5.31]
On the vast royal highway of the sky, as the clouds roam hither and thither,

children.text: pratāyamānā iva pādapāṃsavaḥ patanti mandaṃ paritaḥ payaḥkaṇāḥ // 5.32 //
children.translated_text: the rain-drops fall gently all around, as if they were dust raised by [the clouds'] footsteps. [5.32]
When the circle of lightning-clouds is rumbling, having set the fresh lightning-fire as witness,
the season, as priest, initiates the wedding festival of wave-hand-clasping between rivers and the ocean. [5.33]
Without this season, with its nectar-flows that have brought about all prosperity in abundance,
the earth in its entirety would surely attain the condition of the presiding deity of childless women. [5.34]
When the prince thus spoke eloquently in praise, eagerly describing his own experiences,

children.text: upoḍhalajjā iva diṅmukhāntare tirobabhūvuḥ sakalāḥ payodharāḥ // 5.35 //
children.translated_text: all the clouds vanished into the spaces between the quarters, as if overcome with bashfulness. [5.35]
With the complexion-enhancing ointment of the direction-ladies, with promenades for the free wandering of white-winged birds,
bringing forth the charming bloom of youth of the lotus-ponds — then the autumn season appeared. [5.36]
From the separation from lightning, their graceful beloved, and from the crane of pure birth,
as if sealed in silence by the sorrow of separation, the clouds attained whiteness. [5.37]
When the rainy season, which had obstructed the display of their own qualities, had waned,
the flocks of <s>kalahaṃsa</s> (geese) appeared like joyful laughter of the doe-eyed direction-goddesses. [5.38]
Hearing the clamor of the exuberant white-winged ones (geese), which causes pain to the ears,
the young women separated from their lovers greatly blamed <s>Bhārgava</s> (<s>Śukra</s>) in their hearts. [5.39]
With circles of foam from the boundless ocean, causing the illusion of clusters of <s>Anaṅga</s>'s (<s>Kāma</s>'s) fame,
all the caves and hollows of the directions were filled with flocks of swans with outstretched wings. [5.40]
The masses of pollen expanding all around from the blossoming <s>saptaparṇa</s> (seven-leaved) trees,
with their initial fragrance, created the illusion of scented cosmetic powder on the faces of the direction-ladies. [5.41]
When the elephants in rut were conducting a torrential shower of <s>dāna</s> (ichor-water) in great excess,
even though the rainy season had passed, the great rivers remained exceedingly swollen with water. [5.42]
The lord of the arts (the Moon) spread his radiant net of rays abundantly over the directions,
as if eager to firmly embrace the long-yearning beauty of the white lily ponds. [5.43]
Ruffled by the spreading loads of smiling moonlight, white as fine linen,
the direction-brides, as if bashful at the sight of the king of birds (the swan), appeared to have donned veils. [5.44]
Of the darkness-groves, rich as <s>tamāla</s> tree thickets, whose essence was consumed by the wildfire of the sun,
the autumn cloud-rows appeared like wind-scattered ashes. [5.45]
