The scattered sky, with its loosely wandering autumn clouds, mimicked
the splendor of the salt-ocean at the end of the age, broken by wave-crests of the cosmic waters. [5.46]
First anointed by the cloud-waters, then wearing upper garments of autumn cloud-banks,
their bodies anointed with moon-ray sandalwood paste — the directions wore necklace-strings of stars. [5.47]
Of the direction-brides of lovely garment-splendor, who had recently bathed in the rain-waters,
the stars shone exceedingly, like water-droplets clinging to their bodies. [5.48]
Blossoming from the caress of the moon's hand-rays, the clusters of white lily buds shone,
like clusters of stars whose reflections had entered the clear autumn pond-waters. [5.49]
Blossoming, with revealed thorn-sprouts, releasing honey as joyful teardrops,

children.text: sarojaṣaṇḍāḥ śaradaṃ samāgatāḥ vilokya vismeramukhā ivābabhuḥ // 5.50 //
children.translated_text: the lotus-groves, seeing the arrival of autumn, appeared as if with faces agape in wonder. [5.50]
By the flowing streams of honey from the blossoming lotuses all around,

children.text: agādhatāṃ prāpuratīva pūritāḥ śaratkṛśā apyakhilāḥ sarovarāḥ // 5.51 //
children.translated_text: all the lakes, though shallow in autumn, attained great depth, as if exceedingly filled. [5.51]
With continuous heaps of pearl-essence fallen from the tips of the joints of ripened white sugarcane,
the banks of the noble paddy-field channels attained the likeness of copper-river banks. [5.52]
With fresh seed-children scattered from pomegranate fruits burst open by the abundance of ripening,

children.text: karambitāḥ kānanabhūmayo babhuḥ punaḥ samudyatsuragopakā iva // 5.53 //
children.translated_text: the forest-grounds appeared as if fireflies had risen once again. [5.53]
With fruits bountiful from the ripening of bliss, the paddy-stalks appeared bowing down,
as if increasingly bent with sorrow, contemplating the approaching transformation of their own destruction. [5.54]
With horn-tips marked with scattered mud, their hooves eroding the banks like crescent moons,
bellowing repeatedly, the bulls in their excitement struck the river banks. [5.55]
Meanwhile, the king summoned the prince and addressed him:
"These people, O son, desire to witness your skill in arms." [5.56]

children.text: śrutvā tu tatsūryakulāvataṃsaḥ pratyujjagāda prathamaṃ nṛpāṇām /
children.translated_text: Having heard this, that ornament of the Solar dynasty replied to the foremost of kings:

children.text: ālokyatāṃ tāta! mamāstraśikṣā prāpte dine saptamasaṅkhyayeti // 5.57 //
children.translated_text: "Let my skill in arms be witnessed, O father, on the seventh day from now." [5.57]
Then, when the end of the seventh day arrived, the lord of the people, together with his kinsmen,
took his seat upon the throne to witness his skill in arms. [5.58]
With one lotus-hand holding the bow with its string drawn, with the other an arrow,
the prince, his form clad in armor, appeared before his father. [5.59]

body.text: kiṃ puṣpadhanvā pratimabdhamūrtiḥ, kiṃ vāvatīrṇo madhavān sadhanvā! evaṃvidhā prādurabhūt prajānāṃ vikalpanā vismitamānasānām // 5.60 //
body.translated_text: "Is this the flower-bowed <s>Kāmadeva</s> in youthful form, or has <s>Madhava</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>) himself descended with his bow!" — such were the speculations of the wonder-struck people. [5.60]

children.translated_text: Never before seen, transcending worldly skill, most wondrous — he of incomparable power
demonstrated before his father his manifold skill in arms, that best of heroes. [5.61]
Having seen the skill in arms of the sole friend of the world, unprecedented upon the face of the earth,
the king, whose splendor equaled <s>Indra</s>'s, held himself in high esteem. [5.62]
Thus the steadfast one, having displayed his skill in arms, the foremost among archers, the swift hero,
praised highly by all people from cowherds to nobles for his deeds, returned to his own abode. [5.63]
Together with brides rippling with affection, amidst festive celebrations of song and auspicious ceremonies,
the prince spent some years sporting in the pleasure-houses. [5.64]

body.text: iti buddhaghoṣaviracite padyacūḍāmaṇināmni mahākāvye pañcamaḥ sargaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the fifth canto in the <s>mahākāvya</s> (great poem) named <s>Padyacūḍāmaṇi</s>, composed by <s>Buddhaghoṣa</s>.

Sixth Canto
Description of the Spring Season

children.translated_text: The auspicious spring season appeared, heralding the cooing of bees and <s>kokila</s> (cuckoo) birds,
the quiver of <s>Makaraketana</s>'s (<s>Kāmadeva</s>'s) arrows, the auspicious moment for the issuing of the <s>Malaya</s> mountain breezes. [6.1]
As if frightened by the fierce martial preparation of the formidable staff-bearing [summer],
the sun, with his garland of fierce rays, suddenly turned his horses from the direction of <s>Yama</s> (south) and commenced a northward journey facing the snow-mountains. [6.2]
With a face radiant as the rising moon, proclaiming the command of the Fish-bannered one (<s>Kāmadeva</s>), wearing a pure, most fine garment,

children.text: vanyā vasantasamayena parigrahatvasambhāvitā sapadi puṣpavatī babhūva // 6.3 //
children.translated_text: the forest, honored as a bride by the spring season, suddenly became flowering. [6.3]
To savor the breath-winds of the women folk, whose embrace had grown tighter over time,

children.text: ullāsiteva rasanā kusumadrumāṇām adbhāsate sma navakomalapallavaśrīḥ // 6.4 //
children.translated_text: the beauty of fresh, tender shoots of the flowering trees appeared like a tongue extended to taste. [6.4]
Loosening the bodice of matured leaves, raising the horripilation of clusters of buds,

children.text: ullolayan bhramarakeśabharaṃ latānām udyānabhūṣu vijahāra vasantakālaḥ // 6.5 //
children.translated_text: tossing about the mass of bee-tresses of the creepers — the spring season sported in the garden-grounds. [6.5]
Having mounted the gentle <s>Malaya</s> breeze as his vehicle, as <s>Manobhava</s> (the Love-god) set forth on his conquest of the quarters,
the production of flowers became a shower of fresh parched grain, and the voice of the male <s>kokila</s> became the auspicious conch-blast. [6.6]
The pollen-dust raised high from amidst the forest-rows by the gentle breeze bearing it,

children.text: senāparāga iva digvijayodyatasya cetobhuvaḥ prasarati sma digantareṣu // 6.7 //
children.translated_text: spread across the horizons like the army-dust of the Mind-born (<s>Kāmadeva</s>) intent on world-conquest. [6.7]
The <s>parapuṣṭa</s> (cuckoo) hosts of the flower-weaponed king (<s>Kāmadeva</s>), seeking the mango-blossom arrows that endure the tumult of battle,

children.text: sañcetukāma iva sañcitacārupatrān babhrāma vibhramavaneṣu navāṃkureṣu // 6.8 //
children.translated_text: as if wishing to gather the beautifully accumulated leaves, wandered in the groves of enchanting fresh sprouts. [6.8]

children.text: vīreṇa mārasubhaṭena vibhidya bāṇairbaddhā mahāviṭapināṃ viṭapāntareṣu /
children.translated_text: The flower-clusters, split by the arrows of <s>Māra</s>'s brave warrior, bound in the interstices of the great tree-branches,

children.text: vyākīrṇakeśanicayā iva śatrumuṇḍā vyālolabhṛṅganivahāḥ stabakā virejuḥ // 6.9 //
children.translated_text: With their scattered hair-like petals, shone like the severed heads of enemies — swarming with troops of bees.
The bouquets of flowers, their mouths sealed by bees, their bellies filled with nectar,

children.text: vīrasya māranṛpatervijayābhiṣekaṃ kālena kartumiva ratnaghaṭāḥ praṇītāḥ // 6.10 //
children.translated_text: Appeared like jeweled pots arranged for the coronation of victory of the warrior King <s>Māra</s> (the god of love) in due time.
The freshly blossoming garland of flowers in the areca-palm forest, flooded by the sandalwood-scented <s>Malaya</s> breeze,
Swayed playfully — like a charming fly-whisk garland — by the lord of the mind (<s>Kāmadeva</s>) with the honey [of spring].
The male cuckoos sang their sweet, clear, and melodious fifth-note cries,
Resembling the victory-songs of the bodiless [god of love], in the forest groves upon the fresh mango blossoms.
The <s>Malaya</s> breeze, an unrestrained fragrant elephant, bearing a chain of bee-gifts swelling beyond bounds,
Slowly performed the play of breaching walls upon the mountain-fortresses of proud-hearted women's haughtiness.
The humming of intoxicated bees — auspicious singers for the king of gentle breezes,
Kettledrums adorned with the fragrant mango-elephant, proclamations of the unbridled festival of Love's triumph — swelled forth.
The flood of fresh foliage of the forest trees, expanding all around from root to crown,
Displayed the illusion of spreading young sunlight — to dispel the darkness of the pride of proud women.
With the great rivers of <s>madhūlaka</s> liquor, flowing from the continuously smiling clusters of gems,
The forest attained the state of having a river-mother [i.e., being watered by rivers].
On the banks of the ocean of nectar [i.e., flower-honey], on the charming sand-banks of flower-pollen,
The heroes among bees, moving in circles, began to drink together with their beloveds.
The male bee, having mounted his beloved on a creeper-swing — a playful device —
Whose songs were unfading, joyfully swung [her] with the winds generated by his own wings.
The double-bee (<s>dvirephā</s>), having taken the flower-liquor brought by the cluster of the <s>aśoka</s> branch, with [tender] affection,

children.text: sambhogabhinnāṃ taraṇadvirephaḥ sacāṭukaṃ pāyayati sma kāntām // 6.19 //
children.translated_text: Fed his beloved, whose lips were parted in ecstasy, with sweet flattery.
The baby bees, reaching the bodies of the creeper-ladies, at their cluster-breasts,
Commenced drinking the milk of fresh flower-nectar, forgetting their restless nature.
Having removed the old bowstring, worn from the friction of countless battles, [Love] the burden-bearer
Fashioned a new bowstring for the bow-staff with [a line of] bees from the honey-wand.
As if learning the song of the exploits of the bodiless one (<s>Kāma</s>) from Spring himself,

children.text: śākhāsu śākhāsu mahīruhāṇāṃ śanaiḥ śiśiñjuḥ kalakaṇṭhaśāvāḥ // 6.22 //
children.translated_text: Young cuckoo-chicks softly warbled on branch after branch of the trees.
The mango trees, their upraised branches like outstretched arms, [seemed to]
Proclaim to travelers the command of the ruler of the <s>Śūrpaka</s> [kingdom], with the ear-pleasing cuckoo-notes.
The mature <s>palāśa</s> (flame-of-the-forest) buds, bowing before [him], bore the appearance of golden goads
For the banner-bearing [god of love], who wished to tame the elephant of pride among beautiful women.
The row of blossoms on the <s>palāśa</s> trees, speckled with circling bees,
Attained the radiance of a blazing rock-surface showing its mass of smoke.
The flower-cluster, being drawn by bees greedy for fragrance,
Appeared like the orb of the full moon, swallowed by the mouth of <s>Rāhu</s>.
The breeze, born of the <s>Candana</s> (sandalwood) mountain, because of its association with serpents clinging to the trees on the banks,
Caused lovers to swoon again and again.
In the darkness of the drizzle of honey-drops, the intoxicated male bee,
Amused himself with delight with the eager female bee, as a love-messenger sent by the forest-<s>Lakṣmī</s> to the aroused ones.
The <s>vakula</s>-tree grove, having experienced the consecration of honey-liquor — a mouthful from the mouths of beautiful women —
Bore, on the pretext of new sprouts, the beauty of raised gooseflesh.
In the groves of grafted mango trees, as the <s>Lakṣmī</s> of honey playfully wandered,
The melodious murmurs born from the cuckoos' throats gave a feast to the ears of people — like ankle-bell sounds [of that Lakṣmī].
The <s>kesara</s> (musk-rose) tree, having respectfully drunk the <s>vāruṇī</s> (wine) that fills the lotus-faces of women,
Then disgorged it again, on the pretext of dripping nectar.
In the rivers of fragrance-waves from the trees, filling all the quarters of space,
The gentle fragrant breeze of the <s>Malaya</s> mountain performed a long water-sport.
<s>Manobhava</s> (the god born in the mind, i.e., <s>Kāma</s>), with his strung weapon-bowstring's deep twang reverberating through the sky,
Rained sharp arrows of mango-sprouts, robbing the composure of all worldly beings.
When such was the splendor of the spring month, the prince, eager to undertake a garden excursion,

children.text: rathaṃ samāruhya narendranandanaḥ sahāvarodhena vinirjagāma saḥ // 6.34 //
children.translated_text: Mounted a chariot and went forth together with his harem.
Then, [thinking] 'This is the time to awaken the prince, who has the splendor of <s>Purandara</s> (<s>Indra</s>),'
The deities gradually showed him [beings] whose lives were ruined by old age, disease, and the like.

children.text: krameṇa paśyan purataḥ sthitānamūn nitāntamudvignamanāḥ nṛpātmajaḥ /
children.translated_text: Seeing those [figures] standing before him in succession, the prince, with an extremely agitated mind,
Himself bewildered, asking 'What is this?' — questioned the charioteers who were in the lead.
They too, directed by the gods, in order to cause disenchantment in the prince,
Gradually described to him the transformations of old age and the like, excessively unbearable.
Having heard their words, the prince, his mind thoroughly pervaded by dispassion,
His curiosity for the garden excursion restrained, said to the charioteer: 'Turn back the horses.'
Immediately after that, a treasure-house of austerity, possessed of the disposition of inner peace, was shown before him by the lords of the gods —
[An ascetic] with wide eyes resting upon the crests of waves of the ocean of great compassion.
With a body golden as heated fine gold, wearing a beautiful robe red as broken coral,
With a radiance like the serene full moon, his mind overflowing with abundant friendliness.
And seeing this [ascetic], the foremost among those who practice austerity, the <s>Śākya</s> prince was filled with wonder,

children.text: ka eṣa kā vāsya caritracāturītyapṛcchadabhyāśajuṣaḥ svasārathon // 6.41 //
children.translated_text: And asked the charioteers near him: 'Who is this, and what is the skill of his conduct?'
'This one, O blessed prince, is pure-minded, of sacred conduct, a teacher of the highest truth,
A treasure-house of austerity who has uprooted all sins through his vows — the last among the virtuous [i.e., the final goal of the good].'
'The person who takes refuge in this one's teaching, [which reveals <s>saṃsāra</s>'s nature as] shattered by the waves of old age, disease, and the like,

children.text: krameṇa nistīrya sa janmasāgaraṃ prayāti nirvāṇapadaṃ niruttaram // 6.43 //
children.translated_text: Gradually crosses the ocean of birth and attains the unsurpassed state of <s>nirvāṇa</s>.'
Thus the heroes [among the charioteers], through the influence of the gods, for the purpose of awakening the prince,
Spread the description of the conduct of that treasure-house of austerity — [a description] beyond the reach of speech and mind.
Having heard those words of the charioteers and having found the means for liberation from <s>saṃsāra</s>,
The prince, his inner mind satisfied, yet again wished to make a garden excursion.

body.text: iti buddhaghoṣaviracite padyacūḍāmaṇināmni mahākāvye ṣaṣṭhaḥ sargaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the sixth canto of the <s>Padyacūḍāmaṇi</s> Mahākāvya composed by <s>Buddhaghoṣa</s>.
Seventh Canto: <s>Siddhārtha</s>'s Entry into the Garden.

children.translated_text: Urged once more by the charioteers, whip in hand, the hero among men
Entered a most wonderful garden, delightful to the mind, [beautiful] like the park of <s>Ākhaṇḍala</s> (<s>Indra</s>).
[It was] a school for the singers of the fifth note [cuckoos], a quiver of the bodiless one's (<s>Kāma</s>'s) conceptual arrows,
A treasure-house for the bee-women, and a playground of the <s>Lakṣmī</s> of Spring.
To greet the one who is to be reverenced by all moving and still beings, the trees of the garden,
Their heads bowed by the wind, offering palms joined with fresh shoots, saluted [him].
On the paths strewn with pollen-sand, sprinkled with dripping flower-juices,
With offerings made of fallen blossoms, the hero sported in the midst of the garden.
Seeing the garden grounds with their creeper-necklaces, melodious bee-songs, and the sweet sounds of forest-beloveds as music,

children.text: ārāmabhūmiṃ sa vilokya mene saṅgītaśālāmiva śambarāreḥ // 7.5 //
children.translated_text: He considered it a music-hall of the foe of <s>Śambara</s> (<s>Kāmadeva</s>).
Women with hair hanging to the left, walking slowly to pluck tree-blossoms,
Created the suspicion that tree-goddesses had come to attend upon the prince.
The spring-cuckoos, hearing the conversation of the doe-eyed garden-wandering women,

children.text: vilajjamānā iva baddhamaunāstasthuḥ kṣaṇaṃ tatra vasantaghoṣāḥ // 7.7 //
children.translated_text: Stood there for a moment, as if embarrassed, in bound silence.

children.text: mañjīranādacchalato mamārtiṃ na subhru! kuryā iti nāthateva /
children.translated_text: As if the [<s>aśoka</s> tree], being their lord, [said] 'O fair-browed one, do not cause my pain with the pretext of your ankle-bell sounds' —
One woman slowly touched the <s>aśoka</s> tree with her foot, tender as a lotus.
The <s>aśoka</s> branch, as if unable to endure the touch of the young woman's lotus-foot,
Released [what appeared like] flames of anger-fire, on the pretext of fresh red shoots and blossoms.
One [woman], with the delightful touch of her lotus-hand, cool as moonbeam-light,
Made the mango tree attain the [joy of] a son's arrival — with gooseflesh-like sprouting buds.
The mango branch instantly produced new sprouts with beautiful feathered leaves,
Causes of the pride of the bodiless one [<s>Kāma</s>], tormenters of the wives of travelers.
With the intoxicating ancient honey-liquor, mixed with the fragrance of <s>saugandhika</s> lotuses and blue lotuses, collected playfully within [the flower],
One woman made the <s>kesara</s> tree free from sorrow (<s>aśoka</s>) [i.e., she made it bloom with joy].
With the charming fragrances of the <s>vakula</s> trees, with the self-scattered flower-clusters,
One [woman] fashioned, with a creeper-tendril, an artful girdle of fancy.
Filling her own tresses with the golden flower-nets of fresh jasmine, of noble fragrance,
She seemed to bind the quiver of <s>Anaṅga</s> (Love).
As one [woman], bending a branch with her sprout-like hand, was intent on plucking flowers,
The <s>aśoka</s> branch, as if in anger, veiled her eyes with pollen.

children.text: kareṇa sākaṃ mama komalena spardhāmidaṃ kiṃ paruṣaṃ bhajeta /
children.translated_text: 'Why should this rough [branch] compete with my tender hand?' —
As if seizing with anger, one [woman] playfully broke a mango shoot.
With the pollen-grain of <s>śephālikā</s> flower, sibling [in beauty] to <s>sindūra</s> (vermilion),
One woman playfully made a beautiful <s>tilaka</s> (forehead ornament) on her friend's brow.

children.text: ākṛṣya śākhāḥ sadayaṃ latānāmālūya hastena navapravālam /
children.translated_text: Drawing the branches of creepers tenderly, plucking fresh shoots by hand,
Pushing aside the ruby ornament, the lord [of her heart] placed [a garland] on another's neck.

children.text: kācit pragalbhā ramaṇasya karṇe niveśayantī kila karṇapūram /
children.translated_text: One bold woman, placing a flower behind her lover's ear,

children.text: āveṣṭya kaṇṭhaṃ bhujabandhanena kapolakāntiṃ paricumbati sma // 7.19 //
children.translated_text: Encircled his neck with the bond of her arm and kissed the luster of his cheek.
Some lotus-eyed women, their entire bodies decked with fresh blossoms, looking charming,
Bore the appearance of manifested goddesses of the odd-arrowed one's (<s>Kāma</s>'s) weapons.
Among the creepers — whose cluster-breasts were resplendent, whose leaf-lips were rosy-red —

children.text: madhye latānāaṃ nibhṛtaṃ vasantīṃ sakhīṃ vivektuṃ na śaśāka kācit // 7.21 //
children.translated_text: One [woman] could not distinguish a friend dwelling hidden [among them].
Thus, as the prince with his harem were playfully enjoying the garden excursion,
The thousand-rayed sun climbed to the middle of the sky, as if for the purpose of watching [them].
The breeze, skilled in sporting in the mirage-pools swelling from the touch of fierce heat,
Arrived, announcing the midday, exceedingly intensifying their heat.
The shadows of the trees, spreading all around, as if unable to endure the fierce heat,
Slowly retreated to the root-basins, cooled by repeated water-sprinklings.
On the foreheads of the beautiful women, wearied from their pleasure-excursions,
drops of perspiration appeared, no different from the fame-marks of <s>Pradyumna</s> (the god of love). [7.25]
Drops of perspiration glistened on the cheek-lines of the full-hipped women,
as if dispatched ahead as envoys from the pools, come to fetch them for bathing. [7.26]
Having spent the midday heat in the garden grounds, the guardian of the middle world,
attended by the finest women, reached the pool for water-sport. [7.27]
Its garland of waves, swayed by a gentle breeze, formed swings upon which the lordly geese rocked in delight;
bees floated upon the flood of fragrance emanating from the blooming <s>kalhāra</s> (white water-lily) flowers; [7.28]
Its sweet current of honey-flow descended into the chalice of the night-lotuses;
fish strolled upon the gem-studded terraces of its high, towering waves; [7.29]
In one place, with its fully bloomed fresh white lotuses, it appeared as if joined to the <s>Gaṅgā</s>;
in another, with its split red lotuses, it shone as if embraced by the <s>Śoṇa</s> (river). [7.30]
Its quarters were reddened as if with sindoor by the pollen of lotuses scattered by the wings of birds;
beholding the pool, with its spray forming a pattern of overcast sky, he greatly rejoiced. [7.31]
With their long tresses firmly bound, their lotus-hands bright with golden bracelets,
together with the women of the inner chambers, he, with the majesty of the noose-bearer (<s>Varuṇa</s>), entered the pool for sport. [7.32]
The pool, having first received him who had come with respect, embraced him with wave-hands
and sweetly made inquiry of his well-being with the ear-delighting cries of the <s>kalahaṃsa</s> (swan). [7.33]
When the beautiful women plunged within, the great pool overflowed its banks;

children.text: jalāśayāḥ strīṣu kṛtānuṣaṅgāḥ kathaṃ nu velāṃ na vilaṅghyanti // 7.34 //
children.translated_text: how indeed could reservoirs attached to women not transgress their bounds? [7.34]
The garlands of waves, trembling as if frightened by the impact of the hard, lovely breast-globes of the women,
brought to them offerings of pearls under the pretext of water-drops. [7.35]
In the lotus-lake, the prince sported with the lotus-eyed women,
playfully, like <s>Pracetas</s> (Varuṇa, lord of waters) in the ocean with the women of his inner chambers. [7.36]
The streams of water shot upward from the hands of the beloved women, scattered upon the arms and thighs of their lover,
served for a moment as effortless, gentle fan-waving performed with skill. [7.37]
Some women, their bodies studded with glistening spray, their breast-jar necklaces alternately swinging,
slapped the water gently with their hands, as if striking a lover who had transgressed. [7.38]
While the lotuses, with the songs of bees, performed a dance upon the stage of the waves,
others, with lotus-hands holding seized lotus-stalks, beat the water-drum. [7.39]
The densely filled pool, with the full-hipped women diving and surfacing repeatedly,
shone like the ocean with <s>Apsarases</s> (celestial nymphs) appearing and disappearing within. [7.40]
The prince churned the pleasure-pool with his arm encircled by serpent-like armlets,
as <s>Abjnābha</s> (Viṣṇu, the lotus-naveled one) churned the ocean with <s>Manthādri</s> (Mount Mandara), the bearer of the earth's burden. [7.41]
Streams of saffron-water, propelled by instruments from the hands of the prince,
fell upon the faces of the lovely women, on the lotus-groves, like the first descent of the sun's radiance. [7.42]
The beautiful-browed women drenched him with floods of saffron-water released from jeweled horn-vessels;
thus drenched, he shone exceedingly, like the <s>Pārijāta</s> tree adorned with the glory of new shoots. [7.43]
From the lotus-hand-pump of a certain woman, who had revealed her moonlight-beauty, a stream of water
fell upon the jeweled crown-band of her lord, like the <s>Gaṅgā</s> upon the matted locks of <s>Śiva</s>. [7.44]
A certain rogue, having covered the eyes of one woman with water shot from his own hand-pump,
reverently kissed the <s>bimba</s>-fruit lip of another whose eyes were closed.
From a certain woman nearby, a stream of water playfully directed at the neck of her beloved

children.text: cetobhuvā cittamṛgaṃ grahītuṃ vyāpāritā vāguriteva reje // 7.46 //
children.translated_text: shone like a snare deployed by the mind-born god (<s>Kāma</s>) to capture the deer of the mind. [7.46]
On their faces was the moonlight of a charming smile; on their breasts was the beauty of a waterfall;
at their waists was the grace of a cloud-born river — such was the bathing-water cascade of the beautiful-browed women. [7.47]

children.text: āplāvayāmāsa karodakena vaktraṃ sa kasyāścana mānavatyāḥ /
children.translated_text: He splashed water from his hands upon the face of a certain proud woman;
that very act initiated the procedure of a water-oblation to win over her pride. [7.48]
The breasts of certain women, raised up as they emerged from diving, dripping with streams of water,
shone like <s>cakravāka</s> birds with lotus-fiber stalks drawn out by their beaks. [7.49]

children.text: nirākṛte kāpi taraṅgavātaiḥ stanottarīye sati lajjamānā /
children.translated_text: A certain woman, her breast-cloth removed by the gusts of the waves, being embarrassed,
covered the surface of her breasts, marked with fresh nail-wounds, with a ball of lotus-stem. [7.50]
The lotus-face of a certain woman, rising gracefully from beneath the water as she emerged,
appeared like the orb of the moon rising from the midst of the ocean. [7.51]
When the collyrium decorations of the eyes of the women of the inner chambers were washed away by the waters disturbed during the water-sport,
their lotus-eyes, as if in anger, turned red. [7.52]
The breasts of the lotus-eyed women, with streams of water falling during the water-sport,

children.text: nāgendrakumbhā iva naddhahārāḥ sanirjharaughā iva śailaśṛṅgāḥ // 7.53 //
children.translated_text: resembled the frontal lobes of the king of elephants bound with garlands, or mountain peaks with cascading torrents. [7.53]
The breasts of another lotus-eyed woman, as if they were the great consecration-pots of the empire of <s>Anaṅga</s> (the bodiless god of love),
were drenched by others with streams of water standing in horn-shaped auspicious vessels. [7.54]
With ornaments of coral, topaz, lapis lazuli, emerald, and ruby
fallen from the limbs of the lotus-eyed women, even the lotus-pool became a mine of gems. [7.55]

children.text: evaṃ sa kṛtvā sarasīvihāraṃ sahāvarodhaiḥ sarasīruhākṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: Having thus enjoyed the pool-sport with the women of the inner chambers, the lotus-eyed prince,
emerged and entered the pavilion situated on the bank, where arrangements had been prepared. [7.56]
There, with his devoted circle of friends, wearing specially chosen and varied garments,
the noble prince greatly enjoyed a meal delicious with dishes of superior flavor. [7.57]
The prince then sat within a pavilion spread with variegated silk cushions,
strewn with heaps of flowers, with an auspicious seat placed in its center. [7.58]
There, the son of the lord of the earth, in the pavilion, with the incomparably delightful dances and musical performances of the dancing girls,
with <s>vīṇā</s> (lute) sounds pleasing to the ear and with sweet flute-melodies,
the illustrious one, teacher of the three worlds, spent the remainder of the day. [7.59]

body.text: iti buddhaghoṣacarite padyacuḍāmaṇināmni mahākāvye saptamaḥ sargaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the seventh canto of the <s>Padyacūḍāmaṇi</s> (Crown Jewel of Verse), a <s>mahākāvya</s> composed by <s>Buddhaghoṣa</s>.
Eighth Canto: Description of Sunset.

children.translated_text: Meanwhile, the orb of the sun, gentle in its redness, sank into the western quarter,
like a jeweled mirror playfully drawn from the blue vault of the sky as it slipped away. [8.1]
The helmsman of the afternoon of the sky-ocean, having gathered his net of rays,
carried the sun to the shore of the horizon by means of crystalline oars. [8.2]
The orb of the blazing sun upon the western mountain, coppery like a cluster of <s>aśoka</s> blossoms,
bore the beauty of a coral creeper caught during the churning of the ocean. [8.3]
The sun, as if desiring the journey to the other world, seeing his reflections in lotus-pools,
seemed to have entered the lotus-groves to take leave of his dear kinsmen. [8.4]
Gradually, the solar orb adorned the middle of the western ocean
like the gem called <s>Kaustubha</s> on the emerald-dark chest of <s>Acyuta</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>). [8.5]
Turned back by the whirling current of the other ocean, the orb of the sun
shone as if remounted by the Creator to polish the wheel once more. [8.6]

children.text: mayā vinābdhiḥ pralayaprasaṅgaṃ velā kadācinna vilaṅghiteti /
children.translated_text: "Without me, the ocean would face dissolution and the shore would never be transgressed" —
as if to prove this true, [the ocean] seized the heated, ruddy mass of iron-ore with its wave-hands. [8.7]
The precious sun, its brilliance diminished by the end of day, the examiner [of all things],
was cast into the ocean's burden of embers, as if to be rekindled by the submarine fire. [8.8]
When the lord (the sun) had set, the foster-mother of the day removed the auspicious thread — the garland of bees —
from near the lotuses that had lost their fragrance. [8.9]
As if from the grief of separation from the hot-rayed sun, the lotus-brides began to close;
the row of bees arose from the lotuses like a streak of smoke from the fire of their sorrow. [8.10]

children.text: saurabhyalobhāt savidhe carantī bhṛṅgāvalī padmavaneṣu reje /
children.translated_text: The row of bees, hovering near the lotus-groves out of greed for fragrance,
shone like a snare deployed by the separated lotus-brides to detain [the departing sun]. [8.11]
"The sun has set, abandoning the passionate lotus, my childhood friend" —
as if from excessive attachment, the <s>cakravāka</s> bird, leaving its mate, cried most pitifully. [8.12]

children.text: pratāyamānā prathametarasmin kāṣṭhāntarāle kanati sma sandhyā /
children.translated_text: Spreading out in the first quarter of the horizon, the twilight glowed,
blazing like a flame from the mutual oppression of day and night. [8.13]
The beauty of the sky, seeing the sun set, as if exceedingly agitated by grief,
wearing a rosary-garland of star-pearls, donned the twilight as a saffron-colored ascetic's robe. [8.14]
The tender hands of the wealthy ascetics, gleaming with bracelets of <s>rudrākṣa</s> beads,
closed in homage to the twilight, together with the bee-circled lotus-groves. [8.15]
With an upper garment of blue cloth — the horizons — with the blue-bee pattern of the sky-lotuses,
even as [the sky] entered the house of the earth, the blinding darkness arose. [8.16]
From the moonstone slabs, whose heat was being quenched by oozing moisture,
masses of darkness, like caravan-trains of smoke from the camphor braziers, filled the sky. [8.17]
The twilight darkness, as if to inscribe the laudatory description of the foremost <s>Tārā</s> (star) and the cool-rayed [moon],
darkened the tablet of the cloud-path with strokes of black ink. [8.18]
The darkness, like a mass of radiance from the throat of <s>Śarva</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) performing his twilight-dance,
also covered the sky like smoke from the plants and trees about to burst into flame. [8.19]
The exceedingly dense masses of darkness, cast from horizon to horizon, covered the sky,

children.text: kūlaṅkaṣāḥ prāvṛṣi vārirāśiṃ kalindaputryā iva vāripūrāḥ // 8.20 //
children.translated_text: like the bank-overflowing floods of the <s>Yamunā</s> river filling the ocean in the rainy season. [8.20]
The rows of lamps in the houses shone as <s>campaka</s>-flower ear-ornaments of the night,
as if the rays of the fleeing sun were imprisoned by the most powerful bonds of darkness. [8.21]
Swarms of fireflies wandered about, as if they were spies of the sun investigating the nature of the darkness,
or sparks from the fire of twilight, or clusters of dark gems. [8.22]
With the star-clusters, beautiful like torrential drops spat forth by the cloud-masses of nighttime darkness,
the sky, mottled, took on the beauty of a grove of white water-lilies. [8.23]
With heaps of spray as if scattered from the trunks of unbridled darkness-elephants,
the star-path became gravelly with the brilliant clusters of stars. [8.24]
The sky, dark as a <s>tamāla</s> tree, mottled with star-clusters white as <s>tagara</s> flowers,
stole the beauty of the ocean — drunk by <s>Agastya</s> — strewn with heaps of pearls. [8.25]
The eastern quarter, bearing the moon — that son of the ocean, destroyer of darkness — who was dwelling within the ocean's depths,
gradually became pale in the face, [like a woman in labor]. [8.26]
The rays of the moon, arising while he was still hidden in the ocean, shone forth,

children.text: pītpā pravāhaṃ timibhiḥ sarandhraiḥ śirobhirūrdhvaprahitā ivāpa // 8.27 //
children.translated_text: as if the waters, drunk by the darkness through their pores, were being sent back upward through their heads. [8.27]
The orb of the cool-rayed [moon], half-risen, its mark-beauty slightly revealed,
like a poison-marked half-moon arrow of the conqueror of the three worlds, born of Śṛṅgāra (erotic sentiment). [8.28]
From the tamāla-dark ocean-Viṣṇu, the star-adorned earth-disc [appeared] like a white lotus,
rising from the whirlpool-navel-cavity, charming with barely visible mark-bees. [8.29]
Rising from the midst of the salt ocean, the disc of the lord of stars, free from waves,
bore from that [ocean] being churned the playful beauty of the emerging <s>Airāvata</s>'s forehead. [8.30]
As the garland of cold rays was rising, its disc became coral-red;
that was as if gems, heated by the submarine fire, were placed into the crucible of the ocean. [8.31]
As the lion among kings [the moon] steadily placed its foot upon the slopes and climbed the eastern mountain,
the lordly elephants of darkness, as if frightened, took refuge in the mountain caves. [8.32]
'The radiant one (sun), stumbling at the peak of the western mountain, fell into the other ocean' —

children.text: itīva bhītaḥ kaṭakān kareṇa spṛṣṭvāruroha prathamādriminduḥ // 8.33 //
children.translated_text: as if frightened by this, the moon, touching the mountain-slopes with its hand (rays), climbed the first (eastern) mountain. [8.33]
The newly risen, reddish full-moon disc shone at the horizon's edge,
as if a single seal-mark were impressed by the mineral-fluid applied with the twilight-seal. [8.34]
The lord of night, with his tender hand-rays, [tied] the auspicious-thread garland of bee-rows
around the necks of the eager water-lily pools, near the <s>kumuda</s> (night-lotuses). [8.35]

children.text: ākarṇya gānaṃ madhupāṅganānāṃ karṇāmṛtaṃ pīta ivāmṛtāṃśuḥ /
children.translated_text: Having heard the ear-nectar song of the bee-women, the nectar-rayed [moon], as if drinking [it],
bestowed upon them the sealed nectar-filled bud of the white night-lily cluster. [8.36]
Of the night-woman, whose dark tresses were loosened by the touch of her lord's (the moon's) hand,
the beauty of the sky shone with scattered star-nets like fresh-blown flowers. [8.37]
As if toothed with pearls released from the conch of the ripe moon-disc,
adorned with the spray of the celestial river, the star-studded beauty of the sky shone. [8.38]
When the nectar-rayed lord (moon), passionately, attained the bed-surface of the sky,
the darkness-garment of the dark-bodied woman (night) departed from the midst of the sky. [8.39]

children.text: patiḥ paśunāmiva kālakūṭaṃ patiṃ nadīnāmiva kumbhayoniḥ /
children.translated_text: Like <s>Paśupati</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) [swallowing] the <s>Kālakūṭa</s> poison, like <s>Kumbhayoni</s> (<s>Agastya</s>) [swallowing] the lord of rivers (ocean),
the moon, taking [it] with its tender hand-rays, swallowed the dense darkness. [8.40]
The pale-bodied one with dangling bee-like curls, as if [suffering] from the sorrow of separation —
the moon consoled the <s>kumudvatī</s> (water-lily pool), anointed with honey-flower fragrance, with its hand-rays. [8.41]
With the disc of the hare-marked [moon] arrived as a reflection in the tidal waters resembling jeweled mirrors,
the ocean appeared like the sole treasury of gems, sealed by <s>Varuṇa</s>, the lord. [8.42]
The beauty of the moon-disc, with the inner luster of a young <s>tamāla</s> tree glimmering within, was perceived
as if sealed with the dreadful poison-fluid of the fangs of <s>Rāhu</s> (<s>Saiṃhikeya</s>), whose mouth gapes open to receive his portion. [8.43]
The disc of the deity of the <s>kumudinī</s> (night-lily) clan, clearly displaying the deer-stain mark, shone distinctly
like a whirlpool-circle born from the meeting of the daughter of <s>Kalinda</s> (<s>Yamunā</s>) with the immovable sovereign mountain. [8.44]
The disc of the king of twice-borns (moon), with the deer-mark glimmering within and unbroken radiance, shone exceedingly,
like an ivory ear-disc of the coquettish-browed Night, with its center inlaid with emerald. [8.45]
The moon-disc, internally somewhat stained, resembling the belly of a mirror clouded by moisture and wind,
with its inner space mottled by the spreading luster of the throat — [shone] somewhat like the begging-skull of the Skull-Bearer (<s>Śiva</s>). [8.46]
At the clear evening hour, the prince, whose auspicious ornamental beauty was fashioned by <s>Tvaṣṭṛ</s>,
attended on all sides by courtesans [like] jeweled lamps, returned once more to his own palace. [8.47]

body.text: iti buddhaghoṣaviracite padyacūḍāmaṇināmni mahākāvye aṣṭamaḥ sargaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the eighth canto in the <s>mahākāvya</s> named <s>Padyacūḍāmaṇi</s>, composed by <s>Buddhaghoṣa</s>.
Ninth Canto: The Consecration of the Prince

children.translated_text: Having come home and sat upon the auspicious seat,
the prince received the <s>ārātrika</s> (lamp-waving ceremony) begun by his mothers and nurses. [9.1]
The son of the great king of kings, standing in the pavilion,
he of lion-like build then ascended the throne. [9.2]
Before him, the sweet-formed courtesans with beautiful curls
began to display their wondrous dance-play. [9.3]
His heart unattached to their captivating gestures,
even to the concert and new songs, he gave himself over to inner contemplation. [9.4]
Then the prince shone with upraised <s>cāmara</s> (fly-whisks),
like the ocean with waves tossed up by the wind. [9.5]
The earth-circle was resplendent with jeweled flags and banners,
like the sky covered with many lightning-creepers. [9.6]
The sky, swaying with great smoke-creepers of black <s>aguru</s> (aloe-wood incense),
appeared like <s>Rasātala</s> (the netherworld) strewn with hundreds of black serpents. [9.7]
With sounds that filled the belly of the cosmic egg and deafened all directions,
the sky became inflated by the sounds of numerous kettledrums. [9.8]
Like celestial elephantesses on the stages of the sky, the divine women
performed an unbroken sequence of <s>tāṇḍava</s> (vigorous dance) to the dense sounds of instruments. [9.9]
With their faces adorned by restlessly moving glances,
the firmament seemed to have a thousand deer-marked moons. [9.10]
<s>Vidyādharas</s> and <s>Gandharvas</s>, with <s>vīṇās</s> cradled in their hands,
resounding with ancient songs, proceeded before him. [9.11]
Masses of <s>Mandāra</s> flowers, scattered by the hands of great <s>Indra</s>,
showered down like stars falling from the agitation of the heavens. [9.12]
Thus worshipped by the gods, having traversed thirty <s>yojanas</s>,
crossing the path, he reached the unsurpassed river. [9.13]
[The river] rich with lotus-fiber and leaves enjoyed by swan-women,
its quarters made resonant with the deep roar of <s>makaras</s> (sea-creatures). [9.14]
Its sky dappled with stars of spray-drops from the waves,
its breezes perfumed by the fragrance of lotuses. [9.15]
Its <s>sārasa</s> (cranes) delighted by the bracelet-like ripple-creepers,
with circles of waves neck-deep to the mates of the melodious swans. [9.16]
Colored by the pollen-clusters of <s>kalhāra</s> (white lotus) heaps scattered by fish,
rippling with the honey-flow released from awakened lotuses. [9.17]
As if weaving strands of virtues to cross the great ocean [of existence],
he crossed that river on his steed, absorbed in thought. [9.18]
Having crossed to its sandbank and dismounting from the horse,
he sent back his attendant <s>Channa</s>, giving [him] his ornaments and the steed. [9.19]
[The garb of renunciation], originating from the first cosmic age and gathered by the primordial <s>Brahmā</s> —
the foremost among men adopted the accoutrements of the wealth of austerity. [9.20]
Taking the ascetic's attire, woven with no small virtues,
and covering himself with it, he assumed the posture of one established in austerity. [9.21]
Then, beholding the lord of the world consecrated, the face of <s>Śakra</s>'s direction (the east)
attained a pale glow, as if with gentle joyful smiles. [9.22]
As if by the command of that master, the lord of all worlds,
the direction of <s>Śatakratu</s> (<s>Indra</s>, i.e. the east) assumed a twilight-pink sky. [9.23]
For the very purpose of beholding him, the crest-jewel of the teacher's lineage,
the radiant one (sun), stationed at the riverbank peak, ascended the first (eastern) mountain. [9.24]
'The ignorance of the worlds is thus to be removed by you' —
as if instructing him thus, the sun dispelled the darkness. [9.25]
'The light of knowledge for the three worlds is thus indeed [to be spread] by you' —
as if instructing him thus, <s>Vikartana</s> (the sun) spread forth its light. [9.26]

children.text: dīkṣite bhūbhṛtāṃ nāthe nirviṇṇā iva bhūbhṛtaḥ /
children.translated_text: When the lord of kings was consecrated, the mountains, as if filled with world-weariness,
donned bark-garments, indicated by their reddish-tawny [dawn] appearance. [9.27]
As if from the arising of that sole ocean of enlightenment, kinsman of the <s>Ādityas</s>,
all the lotus-pools assumed the seal of awakening. [9.28]
Pointing toward him who had fulfilled his purpose, as if with palms joined in salutation,
all the <s>kumuda</s> (night-lily) pools stood with closed buds. [9.29]
By the radiance of this guide to the true path, like heretics [before his splendor],
the stars, overcome by the sun's [light], became lusterless. [9.30]
As if to make room for the mass of his fame,
the entire expanse of the directions assumed vast spaciousness. [9.31]
Seeing the cool ray of <s>Siddhārtha</s>'s face shining even during the day,
the moon, as if out of shame, became devoid of luster. [9.32]
As if from beholding him, the sole teacher of the world, the radiant one (sun),
having lost the beauty of its rising redness, entered the sky-hermitage. [9.33]
Fulfilled by the joy of renunciation attained through a hundred heartfelt wishes,
the guide spent some days on the bank of that [river]. [9.34]
Then one day, the first mendicant, hungry and seeking alms,
having traversed a long road, reached the city of <s>Bimbasāra</s> (<s>Rājagṛha</s>). [9.35]
[The city] whose boundary-mountains were surpassed by massive rock-fortifications and <s>sāla</s> trees,
with moats as deep as the netherworld, turning the ocean into mere puddles. [9.36]
Its ground-surface hollowed by the tips of mare-hooves,
its streets muddy with the ichor of intoxicated lordly elephants in rut. [9.37]
With swan-like banners hanging from the eaves of ruby-studded palaces,
resplendent with rows of smoke rising from window-openings. [9.38]
With parrots chattering on pinnacles rivaling the peaks of young mountains,
with mansions whose flag-crests were gently waved by soft breezes. [9.39]
Robust with jeweled arches radiant like <s>Indra</s>'s (<s>Valāri</s>'s) bow (the rainbow),
with garlands of greeting on the streets fashioned from creeper-sprouts. [9.40]
With wide streets as girdles blazing at the center,
with subsidiary lanes aligned with the ripples of monastery-ponds. [9.41]
To collect alms there, the crest-jewel of those rich in austerity,
the leader, wandered slowly through street after street. [9.42]
Though he was the remover of delusion, those who beheld this best of sages —
all, whether naive or learned, fell into the sleep of infatuation. [9.43]
Of those [women] whose eyes were held wide open without blinking,
even he who was the enemy of <s>Manobhava</s> (the god of love) aroused passion in them. [9.44]
Having collected alms there, the one skilled in the rules of training,
quickly repaired to a nearby hill. [9.45]
Charming with <s>kālakaṇṭha</s> (cuckoos) cooing sweetly in its vicinity,
filled with elephants crushed by the blows of lions' paws. [9.46]
Adorned with serpent-lords whose coils resembled the trunks of elephants,
called <s>Pāṇḍara</s>, where flocks of peacocks began their <s>tāṇḍava</s> (vigorous dance). [9.47]
With cloud-travelers resting in the expanse of its wide summit,
its great boulders doubling the appearance of the maddened elephants wandering there. [9.48]
With sky-cavities split open by the tips of massive rocks,
strewn with elephant-pearls wrested by the paws of lions. [9.49]
Its rock-surfaces of golden stone washed clean by waterfall floods,
with <s>Pulinda</s> (tribal) chieftains sporting on its girdle-slopes. [9.50]
Having bathed in a lake close to that [hill], <s>Siddhārtha</s>,
sitting on a stone slab by the shore, partook of the alms-food. [9.51]
The next day, going out from there into the city,
having performed the alms-round ritual, he reached a nearby forest. [9.52]
Near lakes, on river banks, on hills, and in forests —
dwelling there, the venerable one passed many days. [9.53]
In blessed groves of austerity, even difficult-to-accomplish austerities
the firm-hearted one performed for the cessation of worldly suffering. [9.54]
Not attaining the state of <s>Nirvāṇa</s> even by austere practices difficult to perform,
he became anxious, [wondering] 'What method could there be for that purpose?' [9.55]
One day, the manifestation of the ripening of the fortune of his perfections (<s>pāramī</s>) —
the treasury of good conduct beheld the five dreams at dawn. [9.56]
Having seen [them] and awakened, the discerning one, understanding the meaning of the dreams,
"I have resolved that today itself I shall attain nirvrti (final liberation)." [9.57]
Having performed the morning rites and awaiting the time for alms, he
sat beneath a banyan tree honored with worship offerings. [9.58]
Then a certain wide-eyed woman, wishing to propitiate the deity dwelling in that tree,
devoted to offering milk-rice as part of a regular vow, [9.59]

children.text: tacchaṅkayaiva sā tasmai dadau pātreṇa pāyasam /
children.translated_text: suspecting him to be that deity, gave him milk-rice in a vessel.
Taking that, the great being went to the bank of the <s>Nairanjara</s> river. [9.60]
In its waters, clear as the sky on an autumn night, the sage
bathed and ate the milk-rice from the golden vessel, the wise one. [9.61]
Then, in a grove radiant with the glow of young shoots like tender sunlight,
with its green fringes vocal with the charming calls of cuckoos, [9.62]
with creepers delicately swaying on their swings rocked by gentle breezes,
delighting the forest with the joy of tasting young mango shoots, [9.63]
fragrant with nectar streaming from <s>mandara</s> flower buds,
with curiosity aroused by the stirring of the intoxicating fragrance-bearing breezes, [9.64]
with fine paths made golden by clusters of blossoming flower-bunches,
with travelers startled by the buzzing hum of wandering bees, [9.65]
dusty with heaps of pollen scattered by the wings of birds,
with the ground muddied by streams of mango-blossom honey, [9.66]
with breezes carrying blooming jasmine creepers on their trellises,
in the jeweled pavilion of the sovereign empire of the spring season, [9.67]
in a <s>sala</s> forest abundant with <s>tali</s>, <s>tamala</s>, and <s>hintala</s> palms,
the leader of men rested and passed the midday heat. [9.68]
When the end of the day arrived, at the interval of merely one watch,
the Blessed One of great valor arose and approached the <s>Bodhi</s> tree. [9.69]
Taking with his own hand the <s>darbha</s> grass offered by <s>Brahma</s>,
the foremost guide cast it on the eastern ground at the <s>Bodhi</s> site. [9.70]
There, exceedingly soft yet impenetrable by the pride of <s>Kandarpa</s> (Cupid),
the unconquered seat — the great throne — appeared. [9.71]
He ascended the lofty seat, the wondrous enemy of <s>Ananga</s> (Cupid),
like the radiant sun ascending the eastern mountain, the awakener of all beings. [9.72]
The gods beheld him who had ascended the <s>Bodhi</s> seat, of unbreakable virtues,
and began to praise him who was beyond the reach of speech and mind. [9.73]
"Homage to the ocean of jewel-like virtues, kinsman of the sun,
homage to the bridge over the ocean of <s>samsara</s>, abode of sages! [9.74]
Homage to the remover of all afflictions, the capturer of virtues,
homage to the knower of the meaning of all realities, the proponent of non-duality! [9.75]
To him whose eyes overflow with waves of compassion's flood,
to the treasury of good fortune — O Blessed One! — to you, homage! [9.76]
You alone are skilled in shattering <s>Kandarpa</s>'s (Cupid's) pride, and no other;

children.text: pañcānanaṃ vinā ko hi kuñjaraṃ śāsituṃ kṣamaḥ! // 9.77 //
children.translated_text: for who besides a lion is capable of subduing an elephant! [9.77]
You alone are the hero in crushing the irresistibly proud heretics;

children.text: mandareṇa vinā sindhuṃ mathituṃ kena pāryate! // 9.78 //
children.translated_text: without Mount <s>Mandara</s>, by whom can the ocean be churned! [9.78]
You alone are the hero in reducing the ocean of existence to a mere handful;

children.text: kumbhayoniṃ vinā ko hi kovidaḥ sindhucūṣaṇe // 9.79 //
children.translated_text: who besides <s>Kumbhayoni</s> (<s>Agastya</s>) is skilled in draining the ocean! [9.79]
In this, you alone are skilled in awakening the assemblage of disciples;
for who other than the moon can make the lotus-grove smile! [9.80]
You alone, O Lord, are capable of utterly destroying the afflictions of existence;
what other being could remove darkness, save the sun (<s>Haridasva</s>)!" [9.81]
Through these praises of theirs, as his rising virtues were thus glorified,
<s>Manmatha</s> (Cupid) heard of the <s>Buddha</s> seated at the base of the <s>Bodhi</s> tree. [9.82]

body.translated_text: <s>Manobhu</s> (Cupid), agitated in his inner soul upon hearing this, sought to conquer the dispassionate <s>Buddha</s> who scorned worldly attachments —

body.text: ko vābhyupāyo bhuvane mama syādityāśu cintājvaranirduto 'bhūt // 9.83 //
body.translated_text: "What stratagem in the world could be mine?" — and was thus consumed by the fever of anxiety. [9.83]

body.text: iti śrībuddhaghoṣaviracite padyacūḍāmaṇināmni mahākāvye navamaḥ sargaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the ninth canto in the great poem named <s>Padyacudamani</s> composed by <s>Sri Buddhaghosha</s>.
Tenth Canto: Description of <s>Mara</s>'s Battle Preparations

children.translated_text: Meanwhile, <s>Ananga</s> (<s>Mara</s>), impetuous and desiring to vanquish the chief of sages firmly seated at the base of the <s>Bodhi</s> tree,
mounting the maddened elephant named <s>Girimekhala</s>, with his summoned army assembled in full force, marched forth. [10.1]
Marching forth with troops that filled the hollows between the quarters, with the fearsome thunder of victory war-drums resounding like storms,
terrifying all people, with his great army, <s>Ananga</s> gradually descended upon the earth. [10.2]
The excellent conch-blast of <s>Mara</s>'s battle array, being filled by hundreds of frenzied conch-blowers,
caused no distress to the ocean-dwelling <s>Vishnu</s>, whose <s>Pancajanya</s> conch-sound is always cherished in battle. [10.3]
The fierce sound of <s>Makaradhvaja</s>'s (<s>Mara</s>'s) battle-drum, filling the cavities of the entire sky, spreading far and wide,
only brought delight to the god <s>Indra</s>, whose ears feast upon the crash of the thunderbolt. [10.4]
With the cheek-crags of the great mountain ranges shattered by violent wind-force rivaling herds of wild elephants,
with prancing horses tall as cresting waves rising from the ocean of cosmic dissolution, making all directions tremble, [10.5]
with the earth's surface split open by the wheel-rim edges of the advancing circles of chariots,
with dense dust-darkness thick as the gloom of the netherworld, churned by the thunderbolt-like fall of infantry feet, [10.6]
with the sky made meadow-like by the rising terrible dark shadows of brandished swords,
with the entire world deafened by the twanging force of bowstrings from forests of bows playfully curved, [10.7]
with the sky truly earning its name from the terrible uproarious clamor of incomparably fearsome battle-drums being struck,
with the cloud-paths made terrifying by showers of spray trumpeted from the hollows of elephant trunks, [10.8]
with the ocean's waters reduced to mere handfuls by masses of dust ceaselessly billowing from within the earth's depths,
with the interiors of all caves resounding with battle-cries and lion-roars raised by fierce warriors, [10.9]
with the wondrous appearance of autumn brought about by multitudes of waving white <s>camara</s> fly-whisks,
the fourfold army, its wheel set in motion by the furious command of the flower-arrowed lord, gradually advanced. [10.10]
With drum-beats indistinguishable from the deep, terrible, dense thundering of heavy cloud-masses gathering at the end of the <s>kalpa</s>,
blown by <s>Makaraketana</s>'s (<s>Mara</s>'s) musicians, the sound of the war-drums swelled. [10.11]
With dust-clouds rising high from the extraordinary troops, blinding the eyes of the bewildered bull-elephants,

children.text: āviścakāra bhuvaneṣu paraṃ nipīḍāmāḍambaraḥ paṭahajo madanaprayāṇe // 10.12 //
children.translated_text: the uproar of drums at <s>Madana</s>'s (<s>Mara</s>'s) march caused supreme torment throughout the worlds. [10.12]
As the mass of army-dust greatly darkened the faces of the quarters, obscuring even the splendor of the rain-clouds,

children.text: naukā ivoddhurasarasvati naṣṭamārgā bhremurbhṛśaṃ surapathe sumanovimānāḥ // 10.13 //
children.translated_text: the celestial chariots wandered lost in the sky-path, like boats in a turbulent river without course. [10.13]
Amidst the great soldier-dust raised by the wind, the flower-bearing celestial chariots wandered,
like floating fragments of the cosmic egg in the flood-waters of the ocean whirling in the dance of dissolution. [10.14]
Terrified by <s>Kandarpa</s>'s army, fierce as the dreadful winds of cosmic dissolution swallowing all,
the oceans seemed to have flown up to the sky on the pretext of the thick rising mass of dust. [10.15]
Like darkness entering the caverns of mountains split by the tusks of victorious enemy elephants,
the masses of army-dust, beautiful as swarms of bees, expanding without restraint, covered the sky. [10.16]
The cavern of the sky appeared filled to the brim with exceedingly thick floods of limitless army-dust,
as if the middle of the salt ocean were being embraced by the all-inundating floods of the <s>Yamuna</s>. [10.17]
With exceedingly thick nets of dust from the earth's surface rising high, covering the vault of the sky,
the quarters appeared like women who had cast off their dark bodices from fear of <s>Madana</s>'s (Cupid's) arrow-strikes. [10.18]
As the floods of dust, having swallowed the ocean's waters, spread about freely on all sides,

children.text: kalpakṣayo 'miti kaiṭabhajid bhrameṇa bhūyo 'pi viśvamudare parihartumaicchat // 10.19 //
children.translated_text: <s>Kaitabhajit</s> (<s>Vishnu</s>), mistakenly thinking 'This is the dissolution of the cosmic age,' wished once more to contain the universe in his belly. [10.19]
The oceans, swallowed by the harsh dust rising from the earth broken by the hooves of galloping horses,
again became doubly-watered, replenished by streams of rut-fluid flowing from the temples of maddened elephants. [10.20]
The army-dust of <s>Makaraketana</s> (<s>Mara</s>), rising like <s>Kumbhayoni</s> (<s>Agastya</s>) who plunders the ocean's wealth,
eclipsed the sun — as if angry, thinking 'that lord of lotuses is my enemy's kinsman.' [10.21]
The radiant sun, as if unable to behold the extreme insult rising against the banner of his own lineage,
disappeared as the quarters were deeply darkened by successive dense clouds of dust from <s>Kandarpa</s>'s army. [10.22]
With darkness dense from the thick dust of the expanding army, with hundreds of lightning-like flashes from trembling elephant-emblemed banners,
with showers of foam-drops from the horses like hailstones, the march became like the advent of the rainy season, bringing delight. [10.23]
As the unbridled dust spread, deeply darkening the circle of quarters, blocking the expanse of the sky,

children.text: pātālaloka iva bhūvalayo babhūva bhūsanniveśa iva puṇyakṛtāṃ nivāsaḥ // 10.24 //
children.translated_text: the surface of the earth became like the netherworld, and the earth's habitation became like the abode of the virtuous. [10.24]
As all the dust rose exceedingly high from the earth's surface trampled by the hooves of horses,

children.text: bhūmīdharāḥ paramabhūmidharā babhūvuḥ śeṣo 'pi kevalamabhūt phaṇamālabhārī // 10.25 //
children.translated_text: the mountains became supreme mountains, and <s>Shesha</s> himself became merely a bearer of his hood-garland. [10.25]
When the mass of army-dust, expanding, became comparable to the face-veils of the guardian-goddesses of the quarters,

children.text: pāthodhayaḥ sapadi paṅkadhayastadāsan pāthodharā nabhasi paṅkadharā babhūvuḥ // 10.26 //
children.translated_text: the oceans instantly became mud-drinkers, and the rain-clouds in the sky became mud-bearers. [10.26]
As the limitless dust, having drunk up all the waters of the crocodile-teeming ocean, spread through the sky-expanses of the quarters,
the elephants of the quarters breached the boundary walls of the world to make room for its spreading at the <s>Cakracala</s> (rim-mountain). [10.27]

children.text: senāmbudhau jayipadātimahāpravāhe magnāḥ kulakṣitidharā iva vāraṇendrāḥ /
children.translated_text: In <s>Mara</s>'s army-ocean, the great elephants shone like mountain-ranges submerged in the flood of victorious infantry,

children.text: tvaṅgattaraṅganivahā iva tuṅgavāhāa naumaṇḍalā iva rathāḥ sutarāṃ virejuḥ // 10.28 //
children.translated_text: the tall horses prancing like surging waves, the chariots gleaming like flotillas of boats. [10.28]
In the midst, <s>Mara</s>'s spotless victory-banners shone, beautiful with gleaming <s>makara</s> (sea-creature) emblems,

children.text: ambhonidhiṃ nijabalodadhinā vijitya bandīkṛtā iva tadīyapurandhrivargāḥ //
children.translated_text: as if the womenfolk of the ocean had been taken captive, the ocean having been conquered by the ocean of his own army.
His body clad in a dark jacket of smoke-streams born from the great fire of irrepressible fury arising within,
he made himself exceedingly terrifying, with a thousand arms, bearing various weapons. [10.30]
Having filled every mountain-cave across all quarters, resembling the ocean churned by cosmic dissolution,
<s>Makaraketu</s> (<s>Mara</s>) marshaled his boundless, terrifyingly shaped army to an unprecedented scale. [10.31]
Surrounded by his retinue of immeasurable power, covering all quarters and the entire earth,
the self-born one (<s>Mara</s>) approached the chief of sages seated on the <s>Bodhi</s> platform, whose resolve was unshaken. [10.32]
He began to fight him who wore the most beautiful monk's robe, whose neck was gracefully arched as if mounted on the elephant of <s>yoga</s>,
that unshakable mass of valor — <s>Pushpayudha</s> (the Flower-armed one, <s>Mara</s>), with eyes reddened by blazing fury. [10.33]
Near that sage — an ocean of the nectar-waters of tranquility and self-control — the spotless arrows of <s>Smara</s> (Cupid) were released;

children.text: śuddhātmanāmakṛtadānaphalonnatīnāṃ kiṃ kiṃ na sidhyati kṛtākṣayapakṣakāṇām // 10.34 //
children.translated_text: for those of pure soul who have accumulated inexhaustible merit — what indeed does not succeed for them! [10.34]
Against that sage whose body bore the essence of patience, an ocean of steadfastness, fierce as the blazing sun in power,

children.text: kuṇṭhīkṛtātmagatayaḥ kusumāstrabāṇāḥ kṛtyā iva pratinivṛtya tameva jaghnuḥ // 10.35 //
children.translated_text: the flower-arrows, their courses blunted, turned back like failed sorceries and struck <s>Mara</s> himself. [10.35]
The hosts of <s>Mara</s>'s arrows, transforming into flowers, though arriving with wings fully gathered, attained —

children.text: taṃ sthūlalakṣamupagamya na dānalābhaṃ ko vā dadātu guṇahīnaviceṣṭitāya // 10.36 //
children.translated_text: Having approached that one of gross aim who obtained no gift of charity — who indeed would give to one whose efforts are devoid of virtue? [10.36]
Sharp arrows were dispatched by <s>Makaradhvaja</s> (<s>Kāmadeva</s>), who was stationed with his extended bow drawn into a circle,

children.text: āsādya buddhamabhajan sumanomayatvaṃ satsaṅgatiḥ suralateva na kiṃ karoti // 10.37 //
children.translated_text: upon reaching the <s>Buddha</s>, they became flowers — what indeed does good company not accomplish, like a divine creeper? [10.37]
Upon reaching the sovereign sage of peaceful heart, even those arrows devoid of any special consciousness,

children.text: sadyo gateṣu mṛdutāṃ sa hi śambarārirvyāroṣadagdhahṛdayo mṛdutāṃ na bheje // 10.38 //
children.translated_text: at once attained softness; yet that enemy of <s>Śambara</s> (<s>Kāmadeva</s>), his heart scorched by rage, did not attain softness himself. [10.38]

children.text: cetobhavasya saphalā api sāyakāste taṃ prāpya śāntahṛdayaṃ viphalā babhūvuḥ /
children.translated_text: Though the arrows of the mind-born one (<s>Manmatha</s>) were fruitful, upon reaching that one of peaceful heart, they became fruitless;

children.text: daive sameyuṣi parāṅmukhatāṃ hi sarvaṃ hastopayātamapi hanta! vināśameti // 10.39 //
children.translated_text: when destiny turns adverse, alas! everything, even what has come into one's hands, goes to ruin. [10.39]

children.text: itthaṃ jagattrayatiraskaraṇakṣameṣu sarveṣu hanta! viśikheṣu nirarthakeṣu /
children.translated_text: Thus, when all his arrows — capable of subduing the three worlds — had become, alas, futile,
<s>Māra</s>, his heart blinded by the planet of hostility, commanded the wind of the great dissolution to destroy him. [10.40]
Bearing a consecration, as it were, brought about by the mass of water arising from celestial rivers shaken from their very foundations,
the great wind, having gathered flower-pollen as if for worship, reached the unperturbed sage. [10.41]

children.text: taṃ prātya sarvaguṇabhāraguruṃ munīndraṃ na prāgabhavaccalayituṃ sa mahājavo 'pi /
children.translated_text: Having approached that lord of sages, weighty with the burden of all virtues, even that wind of great velocity was unable to shake him;

children.text: naitad vicitramakhilāṭavighasmarasya dāvānalasya na hi mūrchati śaktirapsu // 10.42 //
children.translated_text: this is no wonder — for the power of the wildfire that devours all forests does not intensify in water. [10.42]
Thus, when the great wind, clouds, and other vast weapons had all become futile,
the flower-weaponed one (<s>Puṣpāyudha</s>) again sought to conquer the primeval being with arrows of speech that pierce the heart's vital points. [10.43]
"This seat is by no means yours — it is mine! Rise quickly and depart from there at once!

children.text: āpūritā paramapāramikā mayaiva tatsākṣiṇī mama mahāpṛtanetyavocat // 10.44 //
children.translated_text: The supreme <s>pāramitā</s>s (perfections) have been fulfilled by me alone — my great army is witness to that!" — thus he spoke. [10.44]
The first mendicant (<s>Ādibhikṣu</s>), whose power of austerity blazed forth, extending the tender shoot of his hand from his lap, as soon as he spoke a word,

children.text: māraḥ palāyata tato mahatā balena bhraṣṭātapatrarathaketukuthena bhītaḥ // 10.45 //
children.translated_text: <s>Māra</s> fled thereupon with his great army, terrified, his parasol, chariot, banner, and armor lost. [10.45]
Thereafter, <s>Māra</s>'s women, with languid glances and adorned with tinkling jeweled anklets,
immediately assembled and performed a most magnificent <s>tāṇḍava</s> (wild dance) on the ground before him, in a spacious square arena. [10.46]
Beholding the joy of the <s>Śākya</s> clan, with the essence of <s>samādhi</s> (meditation) composed within, unattached and unshakeable,

children.text: karṇāmṛtāni vacanāni ca kātarākṣyaḥ kāmāṅganā vidadhire karuṇākṣarāṇi // 10.47 //
children.translated_text: the women of desire, with anxious eyes, uttered words that were nectar to the ears, with piteous syllables. [10.47]
"To this one distressed by the falling arrows of love, you who are unable even to bestow the gift of a glance —

children.text: utpāṭya locanayugaṃ dvijapuṅgavāya tvāṃ dattavāniti kathaṃ bruvate purāṇāḥ // 10.48 //
children.translated_text: how do the ancient texts (<s>Purāṇa</s>s) say that you tore out your pair of eyes and gave them to a foremost Brahmin? [10.48]
Submerged in the ocean of the great <s>Makaradhvaja</s> (<s>Kāmadeva</s>), thus tormented by anguish and devoid of support —
unable even to rescue me, how will you ferry the entire world across the ocean of birth? [10.49]
Having seen our most faultless charms, yet keeping far away even a nod of the head in approval —

children.text: ucchīdya mastakamudastaripuprabhāvaṃ tvāṃ dattavāniti vadanti kathaṃ kavīndrāḥ // 10.50 //
children.translated_text: how do the great poets say that you cut off your head, whose power had vanquished enemies, and gave it away? [10.50]

children.text: puṇyātmanāmadhipate! puruṣottamatvamāptuṃ padaṃ tvamabhivāñchasi kiṃ tapobhiḥ /
children.translated_text: O lord of the virtuous! Do you desire to attain the state of <s>Puruṣottama</s> (the Supreme Person) through austerities?

children.text: asmāsu kāmapi vadhūmadhiropaya tvaṃ vakṣastaṭe mahati meruśilāviśāle // 10.51 //
children.translated_text: Place some bride from among us upon your broad chest, vast as the rock of <s>Meru</s>! [10.51]
Or if you desire to attain auspicious progeny or supreme lordship — enough with austerities!
Seat some one among these women — with lotus-wide glances and beautiful curls — on your left side! [10.52]
Of those whose eyes playfully blossom with delight, who seize the pride of clusters of lotuses by the throat,
whose faces glow with radiant smiles — surely only the fortunate become the recipients of their glances! [10.53]
From the charm of speech that attracts, delights, and nourishes, revealed at the end of a glance and drunk reverently by the ears,
from conversation with doe-eyed women — beautiful with wondrous grace and directly experienced bliss — what other nectar could there be? [10.54]
A medicine that endures tireless drinking, a relish in the rising heat born of love, delightful to the mind —
the inexhaustible nectar of women's lips is indeed savored only by meritorious men! [10.55]
With such incomparable dance sequences permeated with the essence of graceful sentiment, and with the charms of their words,
seeing the <s>Buddha</s> whose mind remained unshaken, the young women, overcome with shame, turned back and departed. [10.56]
Thus, the enterprise of conquest of the flower-bowed one (<s>Puṣpaśarāsana</s>) having been rendered barren,
the excellent one, having seated the beautiful [lady of] the grace of perfect enlightenment (<s>Sambodhi</s>) at the foot of the glorious Bodhi tree,
<s>Siddhārtha</s>, having cut off the enemies of defilements acquired through long-standing dispositions,
was consecrated upon the head for the office of protecting the family of the field of liberation. [10.58]

body.text: iti buddhaghoṣaviracite padyacūḍāmaṇināmni mahākāvye siddhārthacarite daśamaḥ sargaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the tenth canto in the <s>mahākāvya</s> named <s>Padyacūḍāmaṇi</s>, the <s>Siddhārthacarita</s>, composed by <s>Buddhaghoṣa</s>.
